en: The Āpastamba Dharmasūtra:

Now, therefore, we shall explain the duties based on customary practice (sāmayācārika-dharma). [1] The consensus of those who know the Dharma is authoritative. [2] And the Vedas are authoritative. [3]

There are four social classes (*varṇa*): the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra. (4) Among them, each preceding one is superior by birth. (5) For those who are not Śūdras and whose actions are not defective, there is the right to receive instruction, the study of the Veda, the establishment of the sacred fires, and the performance of rites that bear fruit. (6) Service to the other classes is the duty of the Śūdra. (7) In each preceding class, the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) is greater. (8)

The initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) is the sacrament for one seeking knowledge, according to the revealed scripture (*śruti*). For the *Brāhmaṇa* states: "The *Sāvitrī* is recited for the sake of all the Vedas. (9–10)

"He who initiates one who is ignorant, and he who is himself ignorant, both enter from darkness into darkness"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. (11) In such a person, one should seek a preparer who is well-born, learned, and composed. (12) And in him alone, whose conduct regarding knowledge and ritual action does not deviate from the sacred laws (*dharma*). (13) He from whom one gathers the *dharmas* is the teacher (*ācārya*). (14) One should never act with malice toward him. (15)
For he indeed produces him through knowledge. That is the superior birth. Only the body do the mother and father produce.

One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the spring, a Rājanya in the summer, and a Vaiśya in the autumn; a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception, a Rājanya in the eleventh from conception, and a Vaiśya in the twelfth from conception. (19) Now follow the optional initiations: (20) in the seventh year for one who desires spiritual luster; (21) in the eighth for one who desires long life; (22) in the ninth for one who desires splendor; (23) in the tenth for one who desires food; (24) in the eleventh for one who desires sensory power; (25) in the twelfth for one who desires cattle. (26)

The time limit for a Brāhmaṇa before he incurs a transgression is until the sixteenth year; for a Kṣatriya, until the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya, until the twenty-fourth—provided they are capable of observing the vows which we shall hereafter describe. (27)

When the time for the Sāvitrī has passed, he should observe the student-life (*brahmacarya*) pertaining to the three Vedas for one season. (28) Now follows the initiation (*upanayana*). (29) Thereafter, for one year, he should perform ritual ablutions with water. (30) Then he is to be taught. (31)

Now, those whose father and grandfather have not been initiated are declared to be equal to Brahmin-killers (brahmahatya). One should avoid their arrival, their food, and their marriage. For those who desire it, there is an expiation (prāyaścitta): as the period for the first transgression is one season, so it is for one year. Then follows the initiation (upanayana), and thereafter the ritual bathing in water.
Thus ends the first section (kaṇḍikā) in the first book (praśna) of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

One should count the years according to each individual, as many as may have not yet entered [the order]. (1) [They should be purified] with the seven *pāvamānī* verses beginning with "That which is near and that which is far," with the *yajus*-purifier, the *sāman*-purifier, and the *āṅgirasa* [purifier]. (2) Or else, simply with the *vyāhṛtis*. (3) Then he is to be taught. (4)

Now, those whose initiation (upanayana) is not remembered from their great-grandfather onwards are designated as belonging to the cremation ground (śmaśānasaṃstuta). One should avoid their arrival, their dining together, and their marriage. If they so desire, the penance is that they should practice the student’s vow (brahmacarya) according to the three Vedas for twelve years; then follows initiation, and thereafter the ritual bathing in water with the Pāvamānī verses and others. Next is the instruction regarding the householder’s life. There is no teaching [of the Veda]. Then, for one who returns [from this state], the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) is performed as in the case of the first transgression. Thereafter, it is according to the natural rule.
The residence of a student in the family of his teacher, having approached him, lasts for forty-eight years. (11–12)

[The guest] should wait for [the host] for up to three days, or until the end of the fortnight, or until the end of the month, or until the end of the year; or he may leave immediately. (13) He may stay for half [of that period]. (14) Or he may stay for one-third [of that period]. (15) [In any case,] he must not stay for less than twelve days. (16) For a religious student (*brahmacārin*) who is there for the sake of learning, there is no obligation to fast with others. (17)

Now follows the rule for the life of a religious student (brahmacarya). ||18|| He shall remain dependent upon his teacher, except in cases that would cause a fall from dharma. ||19|| He shall act for the benefit of his guru and not oppose him in speech. ||20|| He shall sit and sleep on a lower seat than his teacher. ||21||

One should not eat food that has been specially prepared for oneself (22). Likewise, one should avoid alkaline substances, salt, honey, and meat (23). One should not sleep during the day (24). One should not use perfumes (25). One should not engage in sexual intercourse (26). One should suppress self-praise (27). One should not wash one’s limbs (28), except when they are smeared with impurities, and even then only out of the teacher’s sight (29). One should not bathe in water while praising oneself; if one must bathe, one should do so by submerging like a staff (30).

He should have matted hair; [or] he may have a single lock (śikhā) while shaving the rest. The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa is made of muñja grass, triple-stranded, and twisted to the right, provided he has the means. That of a Rājanya is a bowstring; or it may be a muñja-girdle mixed with iron. That of a Vaiśya is a thread of wool; some say it may be made of *sairī* or *tāmalī* fiber.

The staff of a Brāhmaṇa is made of *pālāśa* wood; that of a Rājanya is produced from the trunk of a *nyagrodha* tree with its top pointing downwards; and that of a Vaiśya is made of *bādara* or *audumbara* wood. Some teachers teach that the staff may be made of any tree, regardless of caste.
Clothing: [consists of] hempen, linen, or skins; some teachers prescribe that the garment be dyed with a decoction (kaṣāya).
Thus ends the second section (kaṇḍikā) in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

The garment of a Kṣatriya should be madder-red; that of a Vaiśya, yellow. That of a Brāhmaṇa should be the skin of a black antelope or a black deer. If it is black, he should not lie on a bed or sit on a seat unless it is spread over. The skin of a Ruru deer is for a Kṣatriya; the skin of a goat is for a Vaiśya. [The garment] of wool is for one who belongs to all classes (Sārvarṇika). There is also the woollen blanket. One desiring increase in spiritual power (*brahman*) should wear only skins; one desiring increase in ruling power (*kṣatra*) should wear only garments; one desiring increase in both should wear both—so says the Brāhmaṇa. However, he should always wear a skin as an upper garment.

He does not watch dances. (11) He does not go to assemblies or social gatherings. (12) He is not habituated to gossiping about people. (13) He is habituated to solitude. (14) He does not imitate the teacher’s mannerisms in his own actions. (15) He converses with women only as much as is necessary. (16) He is gentle. (17) He is tranquil. (18) He is self-controlled. (19) He is modest. (20) He is firm in resolve. (21) He is untiring. (22) He is free from anger. (23) He is free from envy. (24)

Bringing all his gains to his teacher, he should go out for alms in the evening and morning with an empty vessel. When begging, he should avoid those of ill repute and those accused of crimes. (25) If women refuse him, the concentrated student (*brahmacārī*) takes away their sacrifice, their gift, their oblation, their offspring, their cattle, their spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), and their food. Therefore, one should not refuse a group of students wandering together; for even among them there may be one who is such as this, observing such a vow—so says the Brāhmaṇa. (26) Alms are not [to be accepted] by inference; rather, they are [determined] by what has been seen and heard. (27) A Brāhmaṇa should beg using the formula beginning with "bhavat" (Lady). (28) A Rājanya should beg using the formula with "bhavat" in the middle. (29) A Vaiśya should beg using the formula with "bhavat" at the end. (30)

Having collected that [food] and set it aside, he should announce it to the teacher. He should eat what is directed by him. In the absence of the teacher, [he should announce it] to the teacher’s family. In their absence, even to other Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*). He should not act for his own purposes.

Having eaten himself, he should wash the vessel. (36) And he should not leave it soiled with remnants. (37) If he is unable to do so, he should bury it in the ground. (38) Or he should cast it into water. (39) Or he should hand it over to an Ārya. (40) Or to a Śūdra who acts as an intermediary. (41)

When away from home, he should eat after having offered alms-food into the fire. Alms-food is commended as being equivalent to an oblation; in that regard, the teacher serves the purpose of the deity, and [the fire] serves the purpose of the *āhavanīya* fire. Having fed him, [he should eat].
Thus ends the third section (kaṇḍikā) in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

That which he eats as leavings is indeed the sacrificial oblation (havis). Whatever other substances he offers according to his availability, these are the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). This is the sacrifice of the religious student (brahmacārin), which is perpetually extended. And one should not give him leavings that are forbidden by the revealed scripture (śruti), such as alkaline substances, salt, honey, and meat. By this, other restrictive rules are explained. For the revealed scripture is more authoritative than customary practice based on inference; moreover, a motive for its application is observed, for satisfaction is experienced [thereby].
One may eat the leavings of one's father and of one's eldest brother. [11] When there is a transgression of dharma, it is not to be eaten. [12]

In the evening and in the morning, he should fetch a water-pot. (13) Having brought firewood from the forest, he should always place it below. (14) He should not go out to fetch firewood after the sun has set. (15) Having kindled the fire and swept around it, he should add fuel in the evening and in the morning according to the instruction. (16) Some say that the worship of the fire should take place only in the evening. (17) He should sweep around the kindled fire with his hand, not with a broom. (18) But before that, he may act as he pleases. (19) He should not perform useless acts with the remains of water used for the fire, nor should he sip water (for ritual purification) with such remains. (20) He should not sip water with water stirred by his hand, nor with water held by only one hand. (21)

And he should avoid sleeping [during the day]. (22) Now, day after day, he should protect his teacher through actions consistent with dharma and artha. (23) Having protected him, when going to bed, he should say: "I have protected the protector of dharma. (24) If the teacher should transgress a rule, whether out of negligence or intentionally, he should point it out to him in private. (25) If the teacher does not desist, he himself should undertake the necessary actions. (26) Or he should cause [the teacher] to desist. (27)

Now, they say that he who rises first and goes to sleep last does not sleep at all. For the student who has thus disciplined himself, even while remaining here, all his actions become fruitful—those which are performed in the life of a householder as well.
Thus ends the fourth section in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the first chapter in the first book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.

The word "austerity" (*tapas*) refers to the observances (*niyamas*). [Sūtra 1] If these are transgressed, knowledge and ritual action flow away from this person, along with his offspring. [Sūtra 2] It results in a state of being like a broken vessel and is detrimental to longevity. [Sūtra 3] Therefore, seers (*ṛṣis*) are not born among later generations due to the transgression of observances. [Sūtra 4] However, some become "learned seers" (*śruta-ṛṣis*) through the residue of the fruits of their past actions upon rebirth. [Sūtra 5] As was the case with Śvetaketu. [Sūtra 6]

Whatever one who is concentrated receives from a teacher, even if it be non-Vedic, the fruit thereof becomes as if it were Vedic. Furthermore, whatever one intends with the mind, speaks with speech, or sees with the eye—whether by forming a resolve, meditating, or looking intently—it comes to be exactly so; thus they teach.

The student’s duties are those which favor the teacher, as well as the rites for prosperity and the completion of his studies. (9) Other duties cease for the religious student. (10) The religious student who maintains his private recitation, delights in dharma, practices austerity, and is upright and gentle, attains success. (11)

Always rising during the latter part of the night, he should stand before his teacher in the morning and offer the greeting: "I am so-and-so, sir. (12) He should also do so for others who are older than himself while residing in the same village, prior to the morning meal. (13) He should also do so upon returning from a journey when they meet. (14) He should do so if he desires heaven and long life. (15)

A Brāhmaṇa should salute by extending his right arm level with his ear; a Rājanya, level with his chest; a Vaiśya, level with his waist; and a Śūdra should salute with his hands joined in añjali at a low level. (16) And for the preceding castes, there is the elision of the name during both the salutation and the formal response to the salutation. (17) But when the sun has risen and he has met his teacher, there must be the clasping of the feet. (18) The salutation itself must always be performed. (19) According to some, one should first clasp the teacher’s feet and then perform the salutation. (20) With his right hand, he should grasp the teacher’s right foot from below, including the ankle, and clasp it. (21) According to others, both feet should be grasped by pressing them together with both hands. (22)

He should be diligently engaged in study throughout the entire day, with no interval between sessions; likewise regarding the duties for his teacher. Even during times when formal study is prohibited, he should study mentally. And he should study whenever he is called upon to do so.
Thus ends the fifth section (kaṇḍikā) in the first book (praśna) of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

At night, he should always help his teacher lie down after washing and massaging his feet. (1) Having been permitted, he himself may lie down. (2) He should not stretch out toward him. (3) Some say that there is no stretching out toward one who is on a couch. (4)

One should not speak while lying down in his presence. (5) But when addressed, one should reply while remaining seated. (6) [One should reply] by rising after him when he stands. (7) One should follow him when he walks. (8) One should run after him when he runs. (9)

One should not sit with shoes on, nor with the head wrapped, nor with hands tucked under the armpits. (10) But one who has set out on a journey may sit so while engaged in his duties. (11) He should not sit too close. (12) He should attend upon the teacher like a god—without gossiping, with a focused mind, and desiring to hear his words. (13) He should not place his knees together [on the seat]. (14) He should stand with the wind blowing from behind him. (15) He should not lean against anything with his hand. (16) He should not lean against anything except for support. (17) If he wears two garments, he should wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*). (18) If he wears only one garment, he should let it hang low in front (*adhonivīta*). (19) He should face the teacher while the teacher faces away from him. (20) He should be neither too near nor too far. (21) He should remain at a distance such that, while seated, he can reach the teacher with his arms. (22) He should not stand directly downwind. (23) When studying alone, he should sit facing the teacher’s right arm. (24) When there are many students, they should sit according to available space. (25) While the teacher is standing, he should not sit unless a seat is provided by way of necessity. (26) While the teacher is sitting, he should not lie down. (27) If he wishes to perform some activity within the teacher's capability, he should do so. (28)

And one should not receive a person of equal standing in his presence (rule 29); nor should one mention him by his lineage (rule 30). Nor should one rise to meet him or rise after him (rule 31), even if he were one's own teacher (rule 32). One should, however, move away from the place and the seat [to show respect] (rule 33). Some say that one may address a pupil of his as "Teacher," even if he is one's own [pupil], by name (rule 34). But toward one who is worthy of respect because of a connection to a teacher—even if he is merely of equal standing—one should behave as toward the teacher himself (rule 35).
Having eaten in his presence, one should not rise and give him the leavings; or, one may rinse one's mouth after addressing him, "What shall I do? ||36–38||
Thus ends the sixth section (kaṇḍikā) in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
He should rise either silently or [with a word of greeting]. He should not turn away from the teacher; rather, having circumambulated him clockwise, he should depart.

One should not look at a naked woman. (3) One should not smell [the scent] after plucking herbs or trees. (4) One should avoid shoes, an umbrella, and a vehicle. (5) One should not smile. (6) If one should smile, one should do so covering [the mouth]; for thus says the Brāhmaṇa. (7) One should not kiss a woman with the mouth. (8) One should not desire her with the heart. (9) One should not touch [her] without cause. (10) "When one is menstruating, when one has blood in the teeth, or when one speaks the truth, one should remain [pure]," for thus says the Brāhmaṇa. (11)

Whatever science he practices under his teacher, those who belong to that teacher’s lineage are also his teachers in that [science]. (12) Furthermore, when he sees others whom he should greet, then these [others] are to be greeted by him. (13)

When several teachers are present and alms have been obtained, the alms belong to whichever one he is following. (14) One who has returned home should give [the alms] to his mother. (15) The mother should cause them to go to the husband. (16) The husband [should cause them to go] to the teacher. (17) Or, he should employ them for religious duties. (18)

Having completed his studies, he should provide the teacher’s fee (*dakṣiṇā*) from righteous means according to his ability, as much as he is capable of. (19) But if the teacher has fallen into distress, he may obtain it even from a *ugra* or from a *śūdra*. (20) Some say that obtaining the teacher’s fee from a *śūdra* or an *ugra* at all times is consistent with dharma. (21) And having given it, he should not speak of it. (22)

And having done it, one should not dwell upon it. (23) One should avoid self-praise and the disparagement of others. (24) When sent on an errand, one should carry out exactly that which was commanded. (25)

And his conduct toward the Teacher is as [toward the Buddha], except for not approaching him [for instruction] (Sūtra 26). Except for receiving [alms food] from him and eating the remnants of his meal, his conduct toward the teacher’s wife is as toward the teacher himself (Sūtra 27). Likewise, he behaves when she teaches him as instructed (Sūtra 28), and likewise toward a senior fellow student (Sūtra 29). With the exception of eating the remnants of the meal, his conduct toward the teacher’s son is as toward the teacher himself (Sūtra 30).
Even for one who has returned home from his teacher, this same conduct regarding these [matters] is based on conventional custom. ||31||
Thus ends the seventh section in the first book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.
Just as is the conduct of a religious student (brahmacārin). ||1||

One who wears garlands, has his face smeared, has his hair and beard anointed, is smeared with unguents, is wrapped or tightly bound, wears a tunic, sandals, or wooden shoes—[these are improper]. (2) One should neither perform nor cause these things to be performed for him during formal acts of deportment. (3) And [this applies] to private activities as well. (4) Such as the cleaning of teeth, rubbing the body, and scraping the nails. (5)

And the teacher should not speak of those substances as being for his own use. But some say that one who has bathed at the proper time according to the rule, whether invited or having arrived on his own, should not turn back from what has been brought to him.

One should not sit on anything higher [than one's teacher] (8). Nor on anything with many legs (9), nor on anything supported on all sides (10). One should not occupy a bed or seat already used by him (11). When commanded, one may mount a vehicle while traveling on a road (12), as well as an assembly hall, a grinding stone, a mat, or a couch (13).

One should not address the teacher with anything other than pleasant words unless one has been addressed first. (14) One should avoid poking at him, laughing at him, addressing him in a familiar manner, calling him by his personal name, or sending him on errands. (15) In times of necessity, however, one may make oneself understood for the sake of a purpose. (16)

Living together, he should go to see his teacher every evening and morning, even if unsummoned. (17) And having returned from a journey abroad, he should see him on that very day. (18) When the teacher and the sub-teacher meet, he should first clasp the hands of the sub-teacher and then desire to clasp the hands of the teacher. (19) The other [the sub-teacher] should forbid him. (20) For in his presence, the honor due to the teacher is suspended. (21) He should visit the teacher’s household for the purpose of seeing him frequently, bringing whatever he can afford, such as tooth-sticks for cleaning the teeth. (22)

In that regard, the conduct toward the teacher is as follows: [Sūtra 23] Desiring him as if he were his own son, and not concealing anything in any matters of duty, the teacher should cause him to grasp the knowledge with great diligence. [Sūtra 24] And he should not, except in times of distress, obstruct him from his studies for the sake of his own interests. [Sūtra 25] A pupil who fails to apply himself skillfully toward his teacher ceases to be a pupil, even though he has surrendered himself to him. [Sūtra 26] Likewise, a teacher who neglects what he has heard [from tradition] ceases to be a teacher. [Sūtra 27]

And he should constantly reproach him for his offenses. Frightening, fasting, touching water, and exclusion from sight are the punishments, applied according to the gravity of the offense until [the offender] desists.
One should grant permission, saying: "Having desisted from other dharmas and having practiced the holy life, may you be immediate [in your realization]. ||30||
Thus ends the eighth section in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the second chapter in the first book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.

Having commenced the term on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, one should not study during the evening for one month. (1) One should cease [the term] on the full moon day of Taiṣya or under the asterism Rohiṇī. (2) According to some, [one should cease] after four and a half months. (3)

One should avoid studying in market-towns. Or one may study in a place smeared with a bull’s dung-pellet. One should not study within the range of a *śamyā*-throw in every direction from a cremation ground. There is no prohibition against studying in a village that has been settled or in a field. However, if that [cremation ground] is known to be present, one should not study in that very location.

A *śūdra* and one who has fallen from his caste are like a cremation ground [for the purpose of study]. (9) Some say this applies when they are in the same house. (10) However, in the case of a *śūdra* woman, there is a suspension of study only during mutual gazing. (11) Likewise, there is a suspension of study during sexual intercourse with another woman of a different caste. (12) When about to study the Veda, if he sees a woman in her courses, he should first converse with a Brāhmaṇa and then converse with her; having conversed with her, he should then again converse with a Brāhmaṇa before studying. In this way, there is the highest welfare for her offspring. (13)

When a corpse is inside [the village], there is no study [for that day]. (14) When a *caṇḍāla* is inside, there is no study. (15) But when those who have carried out a corpse have reached the boundary of the village, there is no study. (16) And when they are seen in the forest, there is no study. (17) And on the day they have returned to the village from outside, there is no study. (18) This applies even if they are virtuous men. (19)

[There is] no study during the night when there is continuous thundering. (20) [There is no study] until the end of sleep when there is lightning. (21) Until dawn, or for as long as one can recognize a dark or red [lightning flash] from the distance of a *śamyā*-throw; while it is lightning at that time, the day along with the following evening is a period of non-study. (22) [There is non-study] due to thunder in the early part of the latter half of the night. (23) According to some, [this applies] after midnight. (24) And [there is non-study] when cattle are being penned. (25) And [there is non-study] for as long as those condemned to death are being executed. (26)
One who is mounted on the back of animals should not study. ||27||
On new moon days, [the observance lasts] for a day and night. ||28||
Thus ends the ninth section in the first book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.

And during the four-month periods [of the rainy season]. (1) The *vairamaṇa*, the *aṣṭākya*, and the *aupākaraṇa*—these are three-day periods of impurity in relation to teachers. (2) Likewise, in the case of kinsmen who are relatives. (3) In the case of a mother, a father, or a teacher, the period of impurity lasts twelve days. (4)

In those cases, there shall be contact with water for that duration of time (V.5). And for those who follow after [the deceased], there is the shaving of the hair (V.6). "Those who have returned from their teacher's house should not shave, except at a place of recreation," say some (V.7). Furthermore, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "This one who is shaven is indeed empty and uncovered; the topknot (*śikhā*) is its covering" (V.8). However, in the case of sacrificial sessions (*satra*), there is the shaving of the topknot because of a specific scriptural injunction (V.9).

Some say that for a teacher, the period lasts three days and nights. (10) For one who has died as a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) before a full year has passed, [the period lasts] one day. (11) Some say this applies to a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*). (12)

When a *śrotriya* approaches, one who desires to study, or is already studying, should study only after having asked for permission; or he may teach. In the presence of his teacher, he should study after saying, "Recite, sir! or he may teach. In both cases—when desiring to study and when having finished studying—he must perform the salutation (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*). Or, while others are studying, if another person should intervene, he should continue studying only after letting out that very same sound.

The barking of dogs and donkeys, the howling of jackals, the cries of the *ekasṛk* and the owl, all sounds of musical instruments, and the sounds of weeping, singing, and the *sāman* chants [constitute an interruption]. (19) Furthermore, there is no study of the *sāmans* according to other recensional branches (*śākhā*). (20) And in all cases involving vocal actions, [there is no study] where these [sounds] might mingle. (21) After vomiting, until one has fallen asleep. (22) Or after consuming clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*). (23) When there is a foul odor. (24) And when sour gruel (*śukta*) has come into contact with oneself. (25) And after eating at the onset of night (*pradoṣa*). (26) And when both hands are wet. (27)

Having eaten food prepared for a *preta*, there shall be no study for the day along with its preceding and following parts; this lasts until the digestion [of that food]. However, one may finish [the meal] with food not intended for a *śrāddha*.
Thus ends the tenth section in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

And at the commencement of a *kāṇḍa*, for one who has no mother; and at the completion of a *kāṇḍa*, for one who has no father. And some say that [one may eat] at the sacrifice of gods who have human natures, after having first eaten [elsewhere].
There is no suspension of study on account of stale rice or raw meat (IV.4). Likewise, there is no suspension on account of medicinal herbs, trees, roots, or fruits (IV.5).

On the day one performs the *upākaraṇa* ceremony for a section (*kāṇḍa*) or composes a *anuvākya*, one should not study that [section] on that day. (6) And likewise, on the days of the commencement and completion of the *pārāyaṇa* of a particular Vedic knowledge (*vidyā*), one should not study it. (7)

When there is a noisy wind on the ground, or when grass is being blown about, or where it rains and streams flow; (8) at the junction of a village and a forest; (9) on a high road; (10) having returned from a journey, one should not study that day until the midday meal; (11) during personal services such as washing the feet, massaging, or anointing with unguents; (12–13) for as long as those activities last, he should neither study nor teach; (14) during the two twilights; (15) likewise when climbing a tree; (16) when immersed in water; (17) at night when the sky is uncovered; (18) and by day when the sky is covered; (19) the recitation of Vedic sections (*anuvāka*) is not prescribed during the months of Āṣāḍha and Vaiśākha; (20) and the daily recitation (*nityapraśna*) is forbidden if performed contrary to the rules. (21)

The rule for that [study] is as follows: Having refrained from the morning meal, having gone to the edge of water, being self-restrained and pure, one should study in a clean place according to the lesson, reciting it aloud; or, when concluding a lesson, one may do so mentally. One should also study mentally during times when study is otherwise forbidden. When lightning is near, during thunder, when one is not in a state of ritual purity, after eating the food of a deceased person, and during mist, they declare that mental study is prohibited. Some say this applies specifically to the time of eating at a *śrāddha* ceremony.

Where lightning, thunder, and rain should coincide outside the rainy season, there is a suspension of study for three days. (27) According to some, this lasts as long as the ground remains wet. (28) Or, according to others, for a period of time following one or two of these occurrences. (29) During an eclipse of the sun or moon, an earthquake, the roaring of waters, a meteoric fall, or a fire portent, there is a suspension of all branches of learning for that entire duration. (30) When there are clouds outside the rainy season, a halo around the sun or moon, a rainbow, a mock sun, or a fish-shaped atmospheric phenomenon; when there is a foul odor in the wind, or during mist—during all these conditions, study is suspended for as long as they persist. (31) Once the wind has ceased, however, it is suspended for only a moment. (32)

[The rule] "near a female jackal" and "when a lizard [is heard]" applies up to the section on dreams (33). At night, one should not study in the forest, nor without fire, nor without gold (34). One should not study a Vedic text that has not been previously taught, nor during the intercalary seasons (35), nor at twilight (36). That which is traditionally prescribed is for all times (37).
As it has been stated elsewhere regarding assemblies: ||38||
Thus ends the eleventh section in the first book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.
Thus ends the third chapter in the first book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.

"Austerity and self-study," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Regarding this it is heard: "Whether he studies his own Veda while standing, sitting, or lying down, he performs austerity; for self-study is indeed austerity."

Furthermore, there is the *Vājasaneyi-Brāhmaṇa*: "This private recitation (*svādhyāya*) is indeed the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*). Its *vaṣaṭ*-calls are when it thunders, when it lightens, when it crashes with thunderclaps, and when the wind blows. Therefore, one should certainly continue to study while it thunders, lightens, crashes with thunderclaps, or when the wind blows, so that there may be no failure of the *vaṣaṭ*-calls. (3) In another recension, the sentence concludes as follows: (4) "Now, if the wind should blow, or it should thunder, or it should lighten, or it should crash with thunderclaps, one should utter a single *ṛc*, a single *yajus*, or a single *sāman*, saying: 'Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! I offer truth into austerity through faith. By this means, his private recitation for that day becomes properly undertaken. (5) This being so, it is not contradicted by the established tradition of the Āryas. (6) For they teach rules regarding what may or may not be studied; that would be rendered meaningless if one were to disregard the *Vājasaneyi-Brāhmaṇa*. (7) Indeed, the established tradition of the Āryas has no discernible cause [for its authority]. (8) It is heard in scripture that the suspension of study applies to knowledge (*vidyā*), but not to the application of mantras in ritual action (*karmayoga*). (9)

The injunctions spoken by the Brahmins—their recitations having been lost—are inferred from their practical application (prayoga). However, where activity proceeds from the perception of pleasure, there is no scripture [governing it]. One who follows such [activity] prepares himself for hell.

Now follow the rules prescribed by the Brāhmaṇas: (13) their praise is that they are "great sacrifices" (*mahāyajña*) and "great sessions" (*mahāsattra*). (14) Every day, one should offer the *balis* to the beings and give gifts to humans according to one's ability. (15)
Thus ends the twelfth section in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

The utterance of *svāhā* for the gods extends as far as the sacrificial wood; the utterance of *svadhā* for the ancestors extends as far as the water-vessel; and [the duty of] sacred study [extends] indefinitely. ||1||

Worship should be performed for those who are superior by caste (2), and for those who are older (3). One who is joyful becomes arrogant; one who is arrogant transgresses the Dharma; and indeed, upon the transgression of the Dharma, there is hell (4).
No instruction exists for one who has returned home. ||5||

The syllable *oṃ* is the gate to heaven; therefore, one who is about to study the Veda should commence with this. (6) And by making other worldly talk, the Veda is turned away [from him]. (7) And at sacrifices, these are the introductory utterances. (8) And in the world, for rites intended for prosperity, there should be sentences beginning with these, such as "An auspicious day! Well-being! Prosperity! (9)

One should not undergo a difficult penance at an improper time, except for the threefold proclamation and the threefold recitation [of the Veda]. Hārīta says that one should proceed without hesitation as far as the Brahman is to be reached.
There is no movement outside the Veda. ||12||

One should attend upon the teacher who instructs what has been prescribed, until the study is completed. ||13|| According to some, one should always attend upon the Arhat. ||14|| No such attendance is required [for other purposes]. ||15|| But for elders, [it is required]. ||16|| When there is a mutual exchange regarding the Veda, no such attendance is required. ||17||

“They say that the Brahman increases,” so they teach. (18) Śvetaketu says: “When he has settled down [as a householder], he should dwell for two months every year in the teacher’s family, concentrated in mind, desiring further learning. (19) “For by this practice, I acquired more learning than in the previous period,” [he says]. (20) But that is contradicted by the scriptures. (21) For when one has settled down [in marriage], the obligatory duties (*naiyyamika*) are prescribed. (22)
Thus ends the thirteenth section in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
The Agnihotra sacrifice, guests, and whatever else is similarly appropriate. ||1-2||

If someone urges him for the sake of study, he should not refuse him, nor should he perceive any fault in that person. If he does not restrain himself when such an opportunity arises, his downfall will surely follow.

Service toward one's mother and father is to be performed as toward a teacher. (6) Upon returning from his studies, all teachers must be saluted by clasping their feet. (7) And likewise upon reunion after having lived abroad. (8) Among brothers and sisters, the same clasping of the feet is to be performed according to seniority. (9)

And daily worship should be performed according to the instruction. (10) One should rise and salute a sacrificial priest, a father-in-law, a paternal uncle, and a maternal uncle who are younger than oneself; or one may simply clasp their feet in silence. (11–12)
Friendship with fellow citizens lasts ten years; that with wandering performers lasts five years;
and one who has been a Vedic scholar for three years deserves to be saluted. 13.

When a difference in age is known, one should salute the elder. (14) One should not salute a teacher while he is on uneven ground. (15) Or, having climbed up after him, one may salute him. (16) In all cases, however, the salutation is performed after rising from one's seat. (17) One should not be saluted by someone who is impure. (18) Nor should one salute someone who is likewise impure. (19) And one who is impure should not return a greeting. (20)

Women who are of equal age [should be saluted]. (21) One should not salute while wearing shoes, with the head wrapped [in a cloth], or with the hands occupied. (22) Women, as well as Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, should be addressed by their pronoun; they should not be addressed by name. (23) According to some, this applies to one's mother and the wife of one's teacher as well. (24)
A ten-year-old Brahmin and a hundred-year-old Kṣatriya:
know that these two are father and son, and of the two, the Brahmin is the father. (25)

He should ask a virtuous person of lower age or a companion about their welfare. (26) He should ask a Kṣatriya about his health (*anāmaya*). (27) He should ask a Vaiśya if he has lost anything. (28) He should ask a Śūdra about his well-being (*ārogya*). (29) He should not pass by a *Śrotriya* (one learned in the Vedas) without speaking to him. (30) Nor should he do so in the forest to a woman. (31)
Thus ends the fourteenth section in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the first book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.

One should wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī) when attending upon teachers, elders, and guests; during the fire-oblation, the recitation of prayers, eating, sipping water for purification, and the private study of the Vedas.

Having sipped water from water that has reached the ground, one becomes pure. Or, one may become pure by having someone who is already pure sip water for him. One should not sip water from raindrops. Likewise, not from water in a hole in the ground. Nor from heated water, unless there is a specific reason.

One who has come from a journey with empty hands should raise his arms and sip water. (7) Within his power, he should not remain impure even for a moment. (8) Nor [should he remain impure] while naked. (9) For one who is already in the water, no purification is prescribed. (10) But having emerged from the water, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). (11)

One should not place fuel that has not been sprinkled with water into the fire. (12) On a bed of grass used by the ignorant, one who is pure should consider himself pure even while not touching others who are impure. (13) The same applies to grass and wood that have been buried. (14) Or, having sprinkled it with water, one may use a garment. (15)

One who has been defiled by a dog should plunge into water with his clothes on. Or, having washed that spot and touched it with fire, and having washed his feet again and sipped water, he becomes pure. One should not sit near the fire while impure. According to some, [one should remain at a distance] of one arrow-length. Nor should one blow upon it. Nor should one place it upon a bed.

A Brāhmaṇa’s residence is lawful in a village that has abundant firewood and water, where he can obtain fuel for himself at will. (22) Having voided urine or feces, having washed away the smears of urine and feces, the smears of food, the smears of impurity from eating, and whatever smears of semen there may be, and having washed his feet and sipped water, he becomes pure. (23)
Thus ends the fifteenth section in the first book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.

One should sip water while standing or while bowing down. (1) Sitting, one should sip water three times with water that reaches the heart. (2) One should wipe the lips three times. (3) Some say twice. (4) One should touch [the mouth] once. (5) Some say twice. (6) Having sprinkled the left hand with the right hand, one should touch the feet, the head, and the sense organs—the eyes, the nostrils, and the ears. (7) Then one should touch water. (8)

But when about to eat, even if already purified, he should sip water twice, wipe his mouth twice, and touch [the lips] once. (9) Having touched the two lips at their dark edges, he should sip water. (10)

One does not become impure by having food remnants on the beard as long as they remain within the mouth, provided one does not touch them with the hand. (11) Regarding those drops that fall from the mouth and are perceived [on the lips], sipping water (ācamana) is prescribed for them. (12) Some say that one need not sip water for those [drops] that fall upon the ground. (13)

Upon dreaming, upon sneezing, upon touching one's nose, eyes, or blood, upon touching hair, fire, cows, a Brāhmaṇa, or a woman, upon walking along a high road, upon touching something impure, upon touching a person who is not pure, upon putting on the waistband (nīvī), or upon putting on the lower garment—one should touch water; or [touch] moist dung, plants, or the earth.
Meat cut with a knife intended for killing is unfit to be eaten. One should not cut off a portion of a cake with one's teeth.

In whose family one dies, food must not be eaten there during the ten-day period of impurity (anirdaśa). Likewise, while the woman who has recently given birth has not yet arisen [from confinement], and while a corpse lies within [the house]. ||18–20||

Food defiled by one who is impure is impure, but it is not necessarily unfit for consumption. (21) However, food brought by a Śūdra who is impure is unfit for consumption. (22) Also, food in which there is hair; (23) or any other impure substance; (24) or that which has been touched by impure things; (25) or where there is an insect that frequents impure places; (26) or a piece of a rat's limb; (27) or that which has been stepped upon by a foot; (28) or by a garment; (29) or that which has been seen by a dog or in an impure vessel; (30) or that which has been brought by a garment; (31) or that which has been brought at night by a female slave. (32)
Or while eating. ||33||
Thus ends the sixteenth section in the first book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.

Where a Śūdra might touch [the food]; or where one eats in the same row as those unworthy [to sit with him]; or where, while others are eating, someone might stand up and offer them leavings or sip water; or where they might serve food after having reviled [the recipient]; or where it has been smelled by humans or other impure things.
One should not eat on a boat; likewise, one should not eat in a palace; rather, one should eat on prepared ground.

One should eat from an earthen vessel that has not been fired. (9) If it has been fired, it must be burnt [until it turns black]. (10) A metal vessel is purified by being scrubbed. (11) A wooden vessel is purified by being scraped. (12) At a sacrifice, purification is according to the traditional scripture. (13)

One should not eat food that has been brought from a marketplace (14). Likewise, one should avoid savory flavors, with the exception of meat, honey, and salt (15). However, one may use oil and ghee after placing them in water (16).

Cooked food that has stood overnight is unfit for eating, drinking, or consuming (17). And so is anything turned sour (18), with the exception of molasses, parched grain, rice, *karambha*, roasted barley flour, groats, vegetables, meat, flour preparations, milk products, herbs, forest plants, roots, and fruits (19). Sour food is also forbidden if it has been mixed with other substances (20).

All intoxicating liquors are unfit to be drunk. (21) Likewise, *ailaka* milk. (22) [The milk of] a camel, a doe, a cow that has recently calved, and a cow in heat. (23) And [the milk] of a cow within ten days of calving. (24) Likewise, the juices of fermented herbs. (25) *Karañja*, garlic, and *parārīka*. (26) And whatever else they declare [to be forbidden]. (27) For the Brāhmaṇa says: "That which is called *kyākv* is unfit to be eaten. (28)

The one-hoofed animals, the camel, the gayal, the village pig, the śarabha, and the cow are [not to be eaten]. ||29|| The cow and the ox may be eaten. ||30|| "The ox is pure," says the Vājasaneyaka. ||31|| The cock is the chief among those that scratch with their feet (vikirāḥ). ||32|| The water-fowl is the chief among those that peck (pratudaḥ). ||33|| [One should avoid] carnivorous animals. ||34|| And the swan, the vulture, the ruddy goose, and the eagle. ||35|| With the exception of the *kruñca*, the *krauñca*, the *vārdhrāṇasa*, and the *lakṣmaṇa*. ||36|| Among five-toed animals, [all are forbidden] except for the monitor lizard, the tortoise, the porcupine, the hedgehog, the rhinoceros, the hare, and the *pūtikhaṣa*. ||37|| The *iṭa* fish is not to be eaten. ||38|| The *sarpaśīrṣī*, the *mṛdura*, the carnivorous fish, and others that are deformed, such as those with human heads. ||39||
Thus ends the seventeenth section in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the first book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.

Honey, raw grain, meat, land, roots and fruits, protection, pasture, a dwelling, and fodder for draft animals—these are things to be accepted even from a person of fierce character. (1) Hārīta says that even these may not be accepted if they have been brought by one who is not a student. (2) Or they may accept raw grain; (3) or food that has been prepared but is tasteless. (4) [In such times] people shall not be well-fed. (5)
If he cannot subsist by his own means, he may enjoy [the property] after giving gold or a beast; he should not settle there permanently; having obtained a livelihood, he should desist.

One who has returned from his teacher’s house must not eat the food of the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya. (9) By nature, the food of a Brāhmaṇa may be eaten; it is forbidden only for a specific reason. (10) Where one performs an act that requires penance, [the food] is forbidden until the penance has been performed. (11) Once the penance has been completed, the food may be eaten. (12) Some say that the food of all castes may be eaten provided they abide by their own dharma, with the exception of the Śūdra. (13) Even in the case of a Śūdra, the food may be eaten if he has been brought to the dharma [of the higher castes]. (14) Having given gold or a cow, one may eat [his food]; one should not settle there permanently, but should desist once a livelihood has been obtained. (15)

The food of the *saṅgha* (monastic community) is not to be eaten. (16) Nor that which is [food] proclaimed [as such]. (17) Nor that of all those who live by their craft. (18) Nor those who live by weapons. (19) Nor those who [live by] poison. (20) A physician. (21) A usurer. (22) An initiated person (*dīkṣita*) before the purchase of the King Soma. (23) Only when the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice has been completed. (24) Or, once the omentum (*vapā*) has been offered, the food of the initiated person may be eaten. (25) Or, when it has been designated for the sake of the sacrifice, they may eat from the remainder; for so says the *Brāhmaṇa*. (26) A eunuch. (27) One who carries out the commands of kings. (28) One who does not offer the *havis* oblation. (29) A spy. (30) And one who has gone forth as a renunciant contrary to the rule. (31) And he who neglects the sacred fires. (32) And he who avoids all [duties], a *śrotriya* who has lost his status, and the husband of a low-caste woman (*vṛṣalī*). (33)
Thus ends the eighteenth section in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

One who is intoxicated, insane, bound, naked, or one who has sat down in protest, as well as one who causes another to sit down in protest, [is not subject to the offense] for that duration of time. ||1||

"Who may eat [the food] of us? [2] "He who desires it," says Kaṇva. [3] "One who is meritorious," says Kautsa. [4] "Anyone at all who gives," says Vārṣyāyaṇi. [5] If the impurity (*rajas*) in a person is stationary, it must be eaten; but if it is mobile, one becomes free from fault through giving. [6] Pure alms should be eaten; thus say Ekakuṇika, Kaṇva, Kautsa, and Puṣkarasādin. [7] The view of Vārṣyāyaṇi is that it should be accepted from everyone. [8] One desiring merit should eat [only what is given by the meritorious]. [9] One should not eat even from a meritorious person if they do not desire to give. [10] One should eat whatever is offered from wherever it comes. [11] "Not without a formal invitation," says Hārīta. [12] Now, they cite two verses from the *Purāṇa*:
Prajāpati considered alms that are being offered, brought forward, and not previously announced as fit to be eaten even from one who has committed evil deeds.
His ancestors do not eat for fifteen years, nor does the fire carry his oblation, he who harbors malice toward her. ||13||
The food of a physician, a hunter, a surgeon, a snarer, an unchaste woman, and a eunuch—these are not to be eaten. (14)

Moreover, they also cite this: "The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the one who eats the food; the innocent man who brings a false accusation [transfers his guilt]; and the thief released by the king [transfers his guilt]—thus there is the mixing of falsehood through begging. (15)
Thus ends the nineteenth section in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the first book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.

One should not practice the Dharma by placing worldly aims in front; for [worldly aims] are fruitless in the pursuit of spiritual elevation (*abhyudaya*). Just as when a mango tree is planted for the sake of its fruit, shade and fragrance arise as secondary effects, so too, when the Dharma is practiced, worldly benefits arise as secondary effects. Even if they do not arise, there is no loss of the Dharma.

One should be free from envy and difficult to deceive regarding the talk of deceivers, rogues, nihilists, and children. [5] "Neither dharma nor adharma exists; neither gods, gandharvas, nor ancestors exist," they say, "This is dharma; this is adharma. [6] But that which the noble ones praise when it is being performed is dharma; that which they censure is adharma. [7] In all regions, one should adopt the conduct of those who are exclusively composed, who are noble, well-disciplined, aged, self-possessed, free from greed, and devoid of hypocrisy—conduct that is consistent with their way of life. [8] In this way, one conquers both worlds. [9]

Trade is not prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa. (10) In times of distress, he may engage in commerce, avoiding articles that must not be sold. (11) These are: human beings, liquids, dyes, perfumes, food, skins, barren cows, phlegm-inducing substances, water, sprouted grain, fermenting agents, long pepper and black pepper, grain, meat, weapons, and the hope for merit. (12) He should especially not sell sesame seeds or rice among grains. (13) Nor is the mutual barter of these items permitted. (14) However, one may exchange food for food, humans for humans, liquids for liquids, perfumes for perfumes, and knowledge for knowledge. (15) He should conduct his business using goods that have not been purchased for trade. (16)
Thus ends the twentieth section in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

[He should subsist] on muñja grass, balbaja grass, roots, and fruits; [he should use] unprocessed grass and wood; he should not become overly attached [to these means of livelihood]; having obtained a means of subsistence, he should desist.

No social interaction is permitted with those who have fallen [from their status] (patita), nor with those who are unworthy recipients (apātra). Now, the causes for falling [from caste] (patanīya): theft, false accusation, killing a human being, neglecting the Veda (brahmojjha), causing an abortion, sexual intercourse with a female relative on the mother’s or father’s side—including those connected by marriage—along with their offspring, drinking liquor, and engaging in forbidden sexual unions.

Having approached the wife of a guru, the female friend of a guru, or other wives of others, some say one does not fall [into sin] for violating the bed of a guru; however, there is a constant practice of unrighteousness [in such acts]. (9–11)

Now, the causes of impurity: 12. Sexual intercourse with Śūdra women by Ārya men; 13. Eating the meat of forbidden animals; 14. [Eating the meat] of dogs, humans, domestic cocks and pigs, and carnivorous beasts; 15. Swallowing the urine or excrement of humans; 16. And for Āryas, consuming the leavings of a Śūdra or having sexual intercourse with a woman who has lost her caste (apapātra). 17. Some say that these also cause loss of caste (patanīya). 18. Other than these, there are various other faulty acts that cause impurity. 19.
Having recognized a fault, one should not report it to others; however, one who has fallen [from his status] should be avoided in matters of dharma.
Thus ends the twenty-first section in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

One should practice internal yogas that are consistent with reason and free from worldly distraction. (1) There is nothing superior to the attainment of the Self. (2) In this regard, we shall cite verses concerning the attainment of the Self. (3)
All living beings are indeed the city of the one who dwells in the cave, who is unharmed day by day and free from stain.
Those who attend upon Him, the immovable One whose abode is the moving world, are immortal. ||4||
Whatever is here in this world called an object of the senses—
the wise man, having shaken off all that, should practice that which dwells in the cave of the heart.
Having found this very Self, practice what is beneficial and not what is harmful;
then, with no further expectation, I shall seek among others the state of the virtuous—the great body of splendor, the Lord established everywhere. (6)
He who is eternal among all beings, wise, immortal, and firm; bodiless, soundless, formless, and intangible—the Great One, the Pure;
he is everything, the supreme goal, he is indeed the equinox, and he is the city of Vaibhājana.
Whoever should practice this in every respect and always act in accordance with it—being disciplined, he who perceives that which is subtle and difficult to see shall rejoice in the world. (8)
Thus ends the twenty-second section in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
Seeing all beings as the Self and reflecting thus, the wise man is not deluded;
he who sees the Self everywhere indeed shines as Brahmā upon the vault of heaven. ||1||
Subtle and more minute than a lotus fiber, he who stands pervading all;
greater than the earth, he who stands firm having encompassed all.
He is the Supreme Lord, distinct from the knowledge of this world by means of the senses, yet not different from the object of knowledge, the one who is manifoldly distributed.
From him all bodies originate; he is the root, eternal and everlasting. ||2||
In this life, the eradication of the humors (doṣas) is rooted in yoga;
having removed those that burn the elements, the wise man attains security. (3)

Now we shall set forth the defects that cause the burning of one's being (bhūtadāhīya). [They are: anger, joy, rage, greed, delusion, hypocrisy, malice, falsehood, gluttony, calumny, envy, lust, resentment, lack of self-control, and lack of yoga; their destruction is rooted in yoga.

Absence of anger, absence of exultation, absence of malice, absence of greed, absence of delusion, absence of hypocrisy, absence of treachery, truthful speech, moderation in eating, freedom from slander, freedom from envy, sharing with others, renunciation, uprightness, gentleness, tranquility, self-control, non-opposition toward all beings, yoga, nobility, compassion, and contentment—these are the rules of conduct for all stages of life. By practicing these according to the prescribed rule, one becomes a partaker of all goals.
Thus ends the twenty-third section in the first book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the first book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.
Having killed a Kṣatriya, one should give a thousand cows for the sake of expiating the enmity; (1) a hundred for a Vaiśya; (2) ten for a Śūdra;
(3) and in each case, a bull is additionally required for the purpose of atonement; (4) and the same applies to women of these [castes]. (5)

Having killed a student of the Veda among the two [higher] castes, or one who has entered a sacrificial session, he is an outcast (abhiśasta). ||6|| And so too for killing a mere Brāhmaṇa. ||7|| And for killing an embryo whose sex is unknown. ||8|| And for killing a woman who is in her courses (an Ātreyī). ||9||

His penance is as follows: having built a hut in the forest, remaining silent, with the head of a corpse as his banner, and covering himself from below the navel to above the knees with a garment made of half-wool and half-hemp, he should follow this rule. His path shall be between two tracks. Upon seeing another person, he should step aside. He should enter a village with a broken, reddish earthenware bowl. He should go for alms to seven houses, asking, "Who [will give] alms to one accused? That is his mode of subsistence. If he does not obtain food, he should fast. He should also tend cattle. A second purpose for being in the village is for their coming out and entering. Having practiced this for twelve years, he is perfected and attains communion with the virtuous. Alternatively, having built a hut on the path of a battle, he may live there seeking to win back the property of Brahmins; having been thrice defeated and then released after winning it back, he is purified. Or, having undergone the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an *Aśvamedha* sacrifice, he is released.

When there is a conflict between dharma and artha, this same [penance] applies to one who chooses artha. Having killed a guru or a learned brahmin (*śrotriya*) engaged in a ritual act, one shall perform this very rite until the final exhalation.
For him, there is no returning to this world; rather, his defilement is cast out. ||25||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

One who has violated the teacher’s bed shall have his penis, together with the testicles, cut off; having placed it in his joined palms, he shall go toward the southern direction from which there is no return. Or, he may attain [liberation] by embracing a glowing iron image of a woman.
A drinker of *surā* should drink *surā* that has been touched by fire. ||3||

A thief, with disheveled hair and carrying a club upon his shoulder, shall go to the king and confess his deed; he should be slain by him, for in being killed, there is liberation. (4) If he is pardoned, the sin touches the one who grants the pardon. (5) Or he may enter the fire, or undergo severe penance. (6) Or he may bring about the end of himself by gradually reducing his food intake. (7) Or he may perform the Kṛcchra penance for a year. (8) Now they also quote: (9)

Having committed theft, drunk liquor, or gone to the wife of a teacher—even without having committed the murder of a Brahmin—they should eat limited food at every fourth meal-time and enter the water for bathing according to the ritual rules. By alternating between standing and sitting, they remove their sin after three years. (10)

Having abandoned the first caste and having destroyed the first caste, he should go and stand in battle; there they shall slay him. Or else, having caused his hair, skin, and flesh to be consumed by fire, he should enter the fire.
For killing a crow, a peacock, a barhin, a ruddy goose, a swan, a crane, a frog, a mongoose, a *derikā*, or a horse, the penance is the same as that for a Śūdra. 13.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth section in the first book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.
And [the killing] of a cow or a bull is [a minor offense] when it is not for a specific purpose; likewise, [it is a minor offense] when other living beings are employed as draft animals or carriers.

Having reviled one who should not be reviled, or having spoken an untruth, one must subsist for three nights on food that is neither milk, nor pungent, nor salted. (3) For a Śūdra, there is a fast of seven nights. (4)
And the same applies to women. ||5||

In the case of those for whom there is a formal accusation, one limb shall be amputated, provided no injury to life has occurred. (6) For acts such as ignoble conduct, calumny, forbidden behavior, eating what is unfit to be eaten, consuming what should not be consumed, drinking what should not be drunk, spilling semen upon a Śūdra woman, or discharging it into a non-vaginal opening; and for performing a blameworthy act either intentionally or unintentionally—one should touch water with verses containing the word *abliṅga*, or with verses addressed to Varuṇa (*vāruṇī*), or with other purificatory texts, according to the repetition of the act. (7)
One who has committed the *avakīrṇin* offense should sacrifice to Nirṛti with a donkey using a *pākayajña* rite. A Śūdra should consume its meat.

[This is] the expiation for studying incorrectly. ||10|| Remaining devoted to the service of his teacher for one year, he should restrain his speech, releasing it only during the private recitation (*svādhyāya*); [he should likewise restrain it] toward the teacher’s wife and when going on a begging round. ||11|| In the same way, for other blameworthy acts that do not cause loss of caste (*apatanīya*), there are further [expiations] which we shall state hereafter. ||12|| Alternatively, he may offer oblations with the words "Desire has done it" or "Anger has done it"; or he should mutter these same words. ||13|| Or, having fasted on the day of the full or new moon while subsisting on sesame seeds, or having fasted [on the following day], he should, on the next morning, touch water and repeat the *Sāvitrī* verse either by means of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) one thousand times, or without breath-control. ||14||
Thus ends the twenty-sixth section in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

On the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, having fasted while consuming only sesame seeds, or on the following day, having touched the water of a great river, he should offer a thousand pieces of wood with the Sāvitrī verse, or recite it; or he should perform sacrificial rites (iṣṭi), sacrifices (yajña), and rituals (kratu) intended for purification.

Having eaten food that should not be eaten, one becomes free from excrement [after purification]. (3) That is attained within seven nights. (4) Or, during both twilights of the winter and cool seasons, one should touch water [for ablution]. (5) Or, one should perform the twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance. (6) The rule for the twelve-night *kṛcchra* is as follows: for three days one eats without oil; for the next three days one eats only by day; for the next three days one observes the vow of eating only what is unasked for; and for the final three days one does not eat anything at all. (7) One should practice this very same rite for a year; that is the "year-long *kṛcchra*. (8)

Now, furthermore: even after having committed many acts that cause loss of caste, one becomes purified by the performance of the penance consisting of three fasts and recitations of the entire Veda. ||9||

One who maintains ignoble conduct on his bed, who bestows interest and drinks fermented liquors, should sit upon blades of grass with his back scorched by the sun after having been saluted like a non-Brahmin. 10.
Whatever black sin a Brahmin commits by serving [a low-caste person] for a single night, [that he cannot undo].
Eating only at the fourth mealtime, one destroys that evil within three years. ||11||
Thus ends the twenty-seventh section in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the first book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.

"Whatever way one regards the property of another as one's own, he becomes a thief"—thus say Kautsa, Hārīta, Kaṇva, and Puṣkarasādi. (1) Vārṣyāyaṇi says that there are exceptions regarding the appropriation [of certain things]. (2) Chaff and fodder for draft animals do not prohibit their owners [from taking them]. (3) Excessive taking is unsuccessful. (4) Hārīta says that in all cases it must be preceded by permission. (5)
One should not go to see a fallen teacher or a relative. Nor should one enjoy any possessions from him. If they meet by chance, one should greet him and then pass by in silence.

A mother undertakes many tasks for the sake of her son; therefore, service toward her must be constant, even if she has fallen from virtue. However, there can be no formal ritual union with her for the purpose of dharma.

Having permitted enjoyments acquired through unrighteous means, and having declared, "Neither we nor unrighteousness [shall remain]," covering himself from below the navel to above the knees, touching water at the three times of day, eating food that is neither milk, nor pungent, nor salty, he shall not enter a house for twelve years. From that, success follows. Then there may be union with the noble ones.
This same [principle] applies to other *patanīya* (causes of downfall) as well. ||14||

But one who has violated the teacher’s bed shall enter a hollow iron image, set it ablaze at both ends, and burn himself. (15) Hārīta says this is false. (16) For he who regards himself as another, or another as himself, becomes indeed a mere accuser. (17) By this very rule, he shall undergo [the penance] until his last breath; there is no restoration for him in this world, but his taint is removed. (18)

One who has violated the rules regarding women shall put on a donkey-skin with the hair turned outward and go for alms, saying, "Alms for one who has violated the rules regarding women," to seven houses; that is his mode of life for six months.

But for a woman who has transgressed against her husband, there shall be a twelve-night practice of the *kṛcchra* penance for that same duration of time. (20) Now, a killer of an embryo, having put on either a dog-skin or a donkey-skin with the hair turned outward, and having taken a human head for the purpose of carrying it against the current [of the river], (21)
Thus ends the twenty-eighth section in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

Carrying a skull-topped staff as his walking stick and proclaiming his deed by name, he should wander about, saying, "Who will give alms to a killer of a learned Brahmin? Having obtained sustenance for life in a village, he should take refuge in an empty house or at the foot of a tree; for there is no association with the noble ones for him. By this very rule, he should live until his final breath. For him, there is no restoration in this world, but his stain is indeed removed. (1)

He who, being heedless, commits a killing when it occurs, [reaps] the fruit of that fault together with his intention; this applies further to other faulty actions as well, and likewise to meritorious deeds.

Even for the sake of investigation, a Brahmin should not take up a weapon. For it is stated in the Purāṇa: "He who kills one who has approached for the purpose of harming him—anger merely touches anger; there is no fault in that."

Now, those who have been accused of such offenses may live together in accordance with the Law, provided they agree to this. They may act as mutual sacrificers for one another, as mutual teachers, and intermarry among themselves. (8) Having produced sons, they should say to them: "Depart from us; for in this way, O noble ones, you will attain the status of Aryas. (9) Moreover, one does not fall [from caste] along with his offspring. (10) This is to be understood by the following: for a person lacking a limb begets a complete-limbed child. (11)

"This is false," says Hārīta. (12) A woman is like a vessel for curd. (13) For when one churns impure milk that has been poured into a vessel for curd, no religious rite is performed with it; likewise, there is no association with that which is produced from impure semen. (14)
Sorcery and the utterance of curses cause impurity but do not entail a fall from caste; however, Hārīta maintains that they do entail a fall from caste.

But for one who commits an act leading to loss of caste (*patanīya*), the penance for acts causing impurity consists of twelve months, twelve half-months, twelve periods of twelve days, twelve periods of seven days, twelve periods of three days, twelve days, seven days, three days, or one day—according to the repetition of the act. Thus ends the expiation for acts causing impurity, according to the practice of the rite.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth section in the first book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the first book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.

Some say that one becomes a *snātaka* by means of sacred knowledge (*vidyā*). (1) Likewise, some say it is by means of a vow (*vrata*) of forty-eight years' duration. (2) Others say it is by means of both sacred knowledge and the vow. (3) In all these cases, the conduct is like that of a *snātaka*. (4) Due to the excellence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the excellence of sacred learning (*śruti*), there is a corresponding excellence in the fruit of worship. (5)

Now, the observances of a Snātaka. (6) He should practice exiting and entering the village by the eastern side, or by the northern side. (7) And during the two twilights, he should sit outside the village, remaining silent. (8) In case of a conflict, that which is characterized by direct Vedic revelation is more authoritative. (9)

One should avoid all dyed garments; likewise, one should avoid those that are naturally black. One should wear a garment that is not dazzlingly bright. And if one has the means, one should not wear a soiled garment. Furthermore, one should avoid covering the head during the day, except when performing the act of voiding urine or excrement.

One should cover one's head while voiding urine or excrement on the ground, having covered it slightly with something else. (15) One should avoid performing the act of voiding urine or excrement in the shade. (16) However, one may void urine upon one's own shadow. (17) One should not void urine or excrement while wearing shoes, nor on ploughed land, on paths, or in water. (18) Likewise, one should avoid the acts of spitting and sexual intercourse in water. (19) One should avoid performing the acts of voiding urine or excrement facing fire, the sun, water, a Brāhmaṇa, cows, or deities. (20) For the cleansing of urine or excrement, one should avoid using stones, clods of earth, fresh herbs, trees, or anything cut from above. (21)
One should not, within the range of one's power, point toward fire, water, a Brāhmaṇa, cattle, deities, a door, or a crosswind. 22.
Moreover, they also cite this: ||23||
Thus ends the thirtieth section in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
One should eat food facing the east; one should discharge excrement facing the south; one should urinate facing the north; and the washing of the feet should be done facing the west. ||1||

One should void urine and feces far from one's dwelling, toward the southern direction or the south-western direction. And after sunset, one should avoid the act of voiding urine and feces outside the village or far from one's dwelling.

One who is impure should not utter the names of the deities (4). One should not speak harshly to either the deities or the king (5). One should avoid touching the feet of a Brahmin or a cow with one's foot (6), as well as doing so with the hand unless there is a specific reason (7). One should avoid speaking ill of cows, sacrificial gifts, or young girls (8). One should not call a cow "stṛhatī" (9), nor should one call a cow that is with her calf "saṃsṛṣṭā" except when there is a specific purpose (10).

One should not say of a non-cow, "It is a non-cow. One should rather say, "It is one that will become a cow. (11) One should not say of what is auspicious, "It is auspicious. One should rather say, "It is meritorious" or "It is excellent. (12) One should not walk over a rope to which a calf is tied. (13) One should not pass between two planks. (14) One should not say, "That one is my rival. If one were to say, "That one is my rival," he would produce a hateful enemy. (15) One should not point out a rainbow to another person. (16) One should not look at falling objects. (17)

One should avoid looking at the sun when it is rising or setting. (18) By day the sun protects living beings, and by night the moon. Therefore, on the night of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), one should especially desire protection for oneself through self-restraint, celibacy, [proper] conduct, and ritual practice. (19) For on that night, the sun and the moon dwell together. (20)
One should not enter a village by a shortcut. If one should enter, one should mutter this verse, "Homage to Rudra, the lord of the dwelling," or another verse addressed to Rudra.

One should not give the remains of food to one who is not a Brahmin. If one should give it, having scraped off [the remnants] with the teeth, one should place them in that [food] and then give it. 22.
And one should avoid anger and other defects that burn living beings. ||23||
Thus ends the thirty-first section in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

One who is devoted to the sacred word should avoid sexual intercourse during the rainy season and autumn. (1) Having engaged in union, he should not lie with her for the entire night. (2) While lying down, he should avoid teaching. (3) Nor should he teach on that same bed upon which he lies. (4)

He should not wear visible garlands or ointments. (5) He should always adorn himself for his wife at night. (6) He should avoid bathing in water with his head on. (7) And he should avoid bathing after the sun has set. (8) He should avoid using a seat made of *palāśa* wood, sandals, and a tooth-cleansing stick. (9) And he should avoid praising his teacher in his presence, such as saying, "You are well-bathed. (10)

One should remain awake during the night. (11) There is no study during the night, except for the instruction of students in the Dharma. (12) Or one may study it oneself mentally. (13) Teaching [others] after midnight is permitted. (14) One should not go to bed thinking, "It is the latter part of the night, so there will be no study. (15) One may sleep at will. (16) Or one may study mentally. (17) One should not frequent small towns or regions inhabited by low-caste people. (18) Nor should one frequent assemblies or public gatherings. (19) If one must enter a public gathering, one should circumambulate it clockwise before departing. (20) One should also avoid entering cities. (21)
And one should not fail to answer a question. Moreover, they also cite this:
The root of one who speaks ill destroys his offspring, cattle, and home; O Dharmaprahrāda, do not speak thus for your own ruin.
Weeping, Death indeed spoke this question. Thus [ends the section]. 24.

One should avoid mounting a donkey vehicle, and one should avoid ascending or descending uneven places. (25) One should cross a river with one's arms. (26) One should also avoid a boat that is in a state of uncertainty [regarding its safety]. (27) One should avoid cutting grass, crushing clods of earth, and spitting without cause. (28) And whatever else they prescribe, and whatever else they prescribe. (29)
Thus ends the thirty-second section in the first book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the first book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.
Thus ends the first question.
From the taking of the hand onwards, there is the vow for the two householders.

Eating at two times [of the day]; (2) lack of satiety with food; (3) fasting on both [the eighth and fourteenth days] of the lunar fortnights; (4) eating only at the time prescribed for fasting; (5) and satiety with food. (6)

And whatever may be dear to these two, that they should eat on this day; ||7|| and they should sleep on the ground; ||8|| and there should be abstinence from sexual intercourse. ||9|| On the following day, there is the *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice offering). ||10|| Its procedure is explained by the [rules for] the *pārvaṇa* sacrifice. ||11|| People teach that this is to be done constantly. ||12||

Wherever one intends to kindle the fire, there one should draw three lines facing east and three lines facing north, sprinkle them with water, and then kindle the fire. Having poured out this water, one should set down another [vessel] to the north or to the east.
The water reservoirs should always remain unfailing with water; this is the vow for the two householders. 15.

One should not sleep during the day. (16) And during the fertile period, one should have union with one's wife in accordance with the vow. (17) Even during the intervening periods, [union] should be only with the wife. (18) And there may be sexual intercourse at the word of a Brāhmaṇa.
