(19) The union should take place while she is still wearing her woman’s clothes. (20) They should share the same bed only as long as the union lasts. (21) After that, they should be separate. (22) [The man] should perform the ritual touching of water. (23)
Thus ends the first section (kaṇḍikā) in the second book (praśna) of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
Alternatively, having washed off the smears and sipped water, there is the sprinkling of the limbs.

For all social classes (*varṇas*), there is supreme and immeasurable happiness in the performance of their own respective duties (*svadharma*). (2) Thereafter, upon returning [to a new birth], by means of the remainder of the fruits of one's actions (*karma-phala-śeṣa*), one obtains caste, physical form, class, strength, intelligence, wisdom, wealth, and the performance of duty. This proceeds like a wheel, revolving through both worlds for the sake of happiness alone. (3) Just as there is an increase in the fruit of seeds of medicinal herbs and forest trees according to the specific qualities of the field and the cultivation, so it is in this case. (4)

By this, the increase of the fruit of demerit has been stated. [Sūtra 5: A Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya who is a thief or one accused of a crime is born in the next world in an immeasurable hell; and when he returns to life, he is born as a Caṇḍāla if he was a Brāhmaṇa, a Paulkasa if he was a Rājanya, or a Vaiṇa if he was a Vaiśya. [Sūtra 6: By these other actions that result in demerit, those who have fallen away are born in wombs that result in demerit for the sake of the degradation of their caste. [Sūtra 7:]

And just as there is a fault in touching, conversing with, or seeing a *caṇḍāla*, so too is there an expiation for that [fault]. (8) For touching [water], it is immersion in water; for conversing, it is conversing with a Brāhmaṇa; and for seeing, it is looking at the luminaries. (9)
Thus ends the second section (kaṇḍikā) in the second book (praśna) of the Āpastamba-dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the first chapter in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

Noble persons, being purified, should be the preparers of the food for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice. (1) One should avoid speaking, coughing, or sneezing while facing the food. (2) Having touched one's hair, body, or clothing, one should touch water. (3)

Or Śūdras consecrated by the noble ones (āryādhiṣṭhita) may be performers of the purificatory rites. For them, the rule for sipping water (ācamana) is the same as that [for the twice-born]. In addition, there is the shaving of the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, and the nails every day. And they must perform the ritual bathing with water together with their clothes. Alternatively, they may shave only on the eighth days or on the festival days (parvan).
When food has been prepared out of sight, one should place it over the fire and sprinkle it with water; that is called "the purification for the gods. (9)
When the food is prepared, standing there, he should announce to the master, "It is ready. The response is: "May that well-prepared, universal food never fail me."

Regarding the offerings and oblations of food fit for consumption by a householder, which are connected with [the attainment of] heaven and prosperity: when these mantras are employed, there shall be sleeping on the ground, celibacy, and the avoidance of pungent and salty foods for twelve days. For the highest [offense], there is a fast for one night.
In the respective place for each of those offerings, one should perform the consecration by wiping with the hand, sprinkling water, placing the offering, and finally pouring water around it. ||15||

One should offer oblations with the hand, using each of the first six mantras, either in the *aupāsana* fire or in the cooking fire. (16) There is sprinkling of water around [the fire] on both sides, as previously described. (17) Likewise, for the *bali* offerings gathered in various locations, there is a single sprinkling of water around [the fire] at the end. (18) When available, they should be performed with food mixed with soup. (19)

To the west [of the center], he places [the fire] with the seventh and eighth [verses], ending toward the north. (20) Near the water-vessel, he places it with the ninth [verse]. (21) In the middle of the house, he places it with the tenth and eleventh [verses], ending toward the east. (22) In the northeastern part of the house, he places it with the four northern [verses]. (23)
Thus ends the third section in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

At the place of the bed, with the *kāma-liṅga* mantra; ||1|| on the threshold, with the *antarikṣa-liṅga* mantra; ||2|| to the north, over the coverlet; ||3|| with the following [verses], in the *brahmasadana*; ||4|| to the south, with the *pitṛ-liṅga* mantra, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*) and with the palm turned downwards, he should perform [the sprinkling]. ||5|| The second [sprinkling] is dedicated to Rudra, as in the case of the other deities. ||6|| The sprinkling for these two is performed separately because of the difference in their ritual rules (*dharma*). ||7|| Only at night, with the final [mantra], [he performs the sprinkling] directed toward the sky (*vaihāyasa*). ||8||
He who, being undistracted, performs these [rites] constantly according to the instruction, attains heaven and prosperity. ||9||

The best portion should be given [to the guest]. (10) One should feed the guests first. (11) [One should also feed] children, the elderly, those afflicted by disease, and women who are pregnant. (12) At the proper time, the two masters should not refuse one who comes seeking food. (13)
"In the absence [of other provisions], there are the earth, water, grass, and kind words;
these indeed are never exhausted in the house of a virtuous person. (14)
When one conducts oneself in this way, the two worlds become infinite. ||15||

To a Brāhmaṇa who has not studied [the Veda], one should give a seat, water, and food; one should not rise up for him. (16) One should rise only for the purpose of greeting him, provided he is worthy of being greeted. (17) This applies to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas as well. (18) When a Śūdra arrives as a guest, one should employ him in work; then one should give him [food]. (19) Or, servants brought from the royal household should honor the Śūdra like a guest. (20)

One must always wear an upper garment. Or else, the sacred thread itself may serve the purpose of the upper garment. Where food is eaten, that place should be swept, cleared away, and sprinkled with water; having scraped off the residues from the vessels and mixed them with water, one should pour them out to the north in a clean spot for Rudra. In this way, the dwelling becomes auspicious.

However, the Brāhmaṇa is traditionally remembered as the teacher. (24) In times of distress, a Brāhmaṇa may study under a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya. (25) And he should follow behind [the teacher]. (26) From that point onward, when traveling, the Brāhmaṇa alone should go in front. (27)
Thus ends the fourth section (kaṇḍikā) in the second book (praśna) of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

On the day one has commenced the study of any of the sciences or the Upaniṣads, there shall be no further study for that day. (1) And having completed the study, one must not depart immediately. (2) However, if he should be in haste, he may go at his pleasure after reciting the lesson in the presence of the teacher; in this way, welfare accrues to both. (3)

If the teacher should approach him after he has completed his studies, the student should go out to meet him face-to-face, clasp his feet, and touch water without feeling any disgust; having placed him in front and attended to him, he should honor him according to the instructions. (4) Whether it be a seat, a bed, food to be chewed, food to be eaten, or clothing, he should remain in a state of service inferior to that of the other. (5) Standing, he should support the teacher with his left hand and cause him to sip water for rinsing the mouth. (6) Or he should do so for another person of superior standing. (7) He should desire to imitate [the teacher] in his standing, sitting, walking, and smiling. (8) When the teacher is nearby, he should avoid urinating, defecating, passing wind, speaking loudly, laughing, spitting, cleaning his teeth, cracking his knuckles, frowning, clapping his hands, and spitting. (9) Regarding the teacher’s wife and children, he should avoid touching them or speaking to them with excessive familiarity. (10)

One should avoid contradicting the words of a teacher with one's own words; likewise, one should avoid contradicting those who are superior, as well as the censure or abuse of any living being, and one should not contradict other branches of knowledge with one's own specialized knowledge.
If one does not shine through that knowledge, one should approach the teacher again and accomplish it through disciplined practice. ||15||

From the commencement until the conclusion [of the term], the teacher must observe restrictive rules. He should avoid the plucking out of hair, meat, performing *śrāddha* rites, and sexual intercourse; or he may have intercourse with his wife during her season. He should be diligent in imparting knowledge to his pupils according to tradition and in adhering to the prescribed rules. Conducting himself in this manner, he secures the welfare of his ancestors, his descendants, and himself. By restraining the outflows through mind, speech, breath, sight, hearing, skin, genitals, and stomach, one becomes fit for immortality.
Thus ends the fifth section in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the second chapter in the second book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.

When there is doubt regarding one’s birth or conduct, one should kindle a fire for the sake of dharma and inquire about that person’s birth and conduct. (1) If he professes his integrity, [the teacher should say]: “Fire is the witness, wind is the listener, the sun is the observer; he professes his integrity. May integrity be his lot, and let this man be free from guilt. Having said this, one may proceed to instruct him. (2)

A guest approaches blazing like a fire. (3) By studying even a single branch of the Vedas in accordance with the sacred law (*dharma*), one becomes a *śrotriya*. (4) One who approaches a householder engaged in his own duty, motivated by righteousness and for no other purpose, is a guest (*atithi*). (5) Through honoring him, there is peace and heaven. (6)

Having approached him face-to-face and greeted him according to his age, he should offer him a seat. (7) Some say that within one's capacity, the seat should not have many legs. (8) He should wash his feet; some say this should be done by a *śūdra* couple. (9) One of them should perform the washing. (10) He should offer him water; some say it should be in an earthen vessel. (11) One who has not yet returned home from his teacher (*asamāvṛtta*) should not offer water. (12) In this case, the exchange of recitation (*adhyayana-sāṃvṛtti*) is additionally required. (13) Having comforted him, he should satisfy him with juices, foods, and water, at least with the lowest quality. (14) He should provide a dwelling, a bed above, a mattress, a pillow, a coverlet, and ointment. (15)

Having summoned the food-preparer, he should pour out rice or barley for that purpose. (16) He should look at the prepared foods, saying: "Is this more, or is this [more]? (17) He should say only: "Make it more. (18)

One should not eat the food of one who hates him, or of one who hates others, nor of one who suspects him of a fault, or of one who has been suspected of a fault. For it is known from scripture: "He indeed consumes the evil of that person."
Thus ends the sixth section in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

This very sacrifice of the householder belongs to Prajāpati; it is perpetually extended. (1) That fire which is for guests is the Āhavanīya; that which is in the household is the Gārhapatya; and that on which food is cooked is the Anvāhāryapacana. (2) He who eats before his guest eats away the vigor, nourishment, progeny, cattle, and the merit of his sacrifices and charitable works belonging to the house. (3) Food with a libation of milk is equal to the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; with clarified butter, it is equal to the Ukthya; with honey, it is equal to the Atirātra; and with meat, it is equal to the Dvādaśāha; and with water, there is an increase of progeny and long life. (4) It is known from scripture that both dear and unpleasant guests cause one to go to the heavenly world. (5) When he gives [food] in the morning, at midday, and in the evening, these become the Soma-pressings (savana). (6) When he attends to their needs, that is the ritual conclusion (udavasyati). (7) When he offers them consolation, that is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and the praise. (8) When he accomplishes their business, those are the Viṣṇu-strides (viṣṇukrama). (9) When he turns back [to depart], that is the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha). (10) Thus says the Brāhmaṇa. (11) If a king arrives as a guest, he should have a more exalted honor performed for him than for himself. (12) If a guest arrives at the house of one who maintains the sacred fires (āhitāgni), he should rise to meet him in person and say: "O Vratya, where did you stay? "O Vratya, here is water. "O Vratya, may you be satisfied. (13) Before the Agnihotra oblation is offered, he should mutter softly: "O Vratya, may it be according to your mind"; "O Vratya, may it be according to your will"; "O Vratya, may it be according to what is dear to you"; "O Vratya, may it be according to your desire. (14) If a guest should arrive when the fires have been taken out but before the oblations have been offered, he should rise to meet him in person and say: "O Vratya, give me leave; I shall offer the oblation. Only when thus permitted should he offer. If he should offer without being permitted, the Brāhmaṇa declares it to be a fault. (15)

It is known from the sacred tradition: "If one should lodge guests for one night, he conquers the worlds of the earth; by a second night, the worlds of the intermediate space; by a third, the worlds of heaven; by a fourth, the distant worlds; and by an unlimited number of nights, he conquers unlimited worlds."

If a guest who is not a *samudeta* should arrive claiming to be one, he should give him a seat, water, and food, saying, "I am giving this to a *śrotriya*. In this way, his [act] becomes successful. ||17||
Thus ends the seventh section in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the third chapter in the second book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.
One should not rise up or descend from one's seat for a guest who has already made his dwelling; however, if he has been greeted first, one should do so. ||1||

The remainder [of the meal] should be for those guests who are entitled to eat it. (2) One should not eat savory foods in the house unless some have been left over for the guests. (3) One should not cook delicious food for one’s own sake. (4)

One who has studied the Veda is worthy of the cow and the honey-mixture (madhuparka). [5] An *ācārya*, an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), a graduate (*snātaka*), or a righteous king [is also worthy]. [6] For an *ācārya*, an officiating priest, a father-in-law, and a king—if they have come to visit after a year has passed—a cow and a honey-mixture are to be offered. [7] A honey-mixture consists of curds mixed with honey, or milk mixed with honey. [8] In the absence of these, water [is used]. [9]

The Veda has six ancillaries (aṅgas): [Sūtra 10] Prosody (chandas), ritual science (kalpa), grammar (vyākaraṇa), astronomy (jyotiṣa), etymology (nirukta), and phonetics (śīkṣā)—these are the six [Sūtra 11]. However, the word "Veda" applies to those actions which have words and meanings as their starting point, upon the completion of the traditional collection (samāmnāya). In that regard, the aforementioned number [of six] is contradicted [by the existence of more texts] [Sūtra 12]. But it is the consensus of those who know the principles of logic that the ancillaries are not designated by the same name as the primary [Vedas] [Sūtra 13].
If, having set aside a guest, one remembers him after the meal has begun, one should desist from eating, fast for that day, and [make amends]. ||14||
Thus ends the eighth section in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

On the following day, having gratified [the officiants] according to his desire, he should accomplish [the rite]. (1) [He should follow] one who has a vehicle as far as the vehicle [reaches]. (2) [He should follow] as long as the other does not give permission [to depart]. (3) In the absence of a visible boundary, he should turn back at the boundary. (4)

One should make all [beings], down to the dogs and the *cāṇḍālas*, sharers in the *vaiśvadeva* offering. (5) Some say that one should not give to those who are unworthy. (6) One who has been initiated (*upeta*) should avoid the leavings of women and of one who has not been initiated. (7)

All gifts are preceded by water [libations]. (8) In the monastery, [the distribution] is according to the sacred tradition. (9) A share is ordained for those who are permanent residents and partakers, provided it does not cause them hardship. (10) One may certainly deprive oneself, one's wife, or one's son [of food], but never a slave or a laborer. (11) Furthermore, one should ensure that one’s own sustenance is not so restricted that one becomes incapable of performing one’s duties. (12) Moreover, they cite this: "Eight mouthfuls are the meal of a sage; sixteen for a forest-dweller; thirty-two for a householder; and an unlimited amount for a student. (13)
The maintainer of the sacred fires, the ox, and the student—these three succeed only while eating;
for them there is no success through fasting. (13)
Thus ends the ninth section in the second book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the second book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.

The occasions for begging are: [the need for] a teacher, marriage, a sacrifice, the desire to support one's mother and father, and the prevention of the violation of a vow by an Arhat. (1) In those cases, having considered the merits [of the recipient], one should give according to one's ability. (2) However, begging for the sake of gratifying the senses is without occasion; one should not heed that. (3)

The specific duties of a Brāhmaṇa are: studying and teaching, sacrificing and officiating at sacrifices, giving and receiving gifts, inheritance, and gleaning ears of grain or picking up single grains. (4) Furthermore, anything else that has not been previously claimed [as one's own]. (5)

For a Kṣatriya, these same duties apply, with the exception of teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts; however, they include the additional duties of administering punishment and engaging in battle.
The duties of the Vaiśya are indeed like those of the Kṣatriya, with the exception of the staff and warfare, and with the addition of agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade. (7)
One does not choose as a sacrificial priest one who has not studied the Vedas, nor one who is haggling for a fee. One who has not studied the Vedas is unworthy of performing sacrifices.

In battle, one should act in accordance with the methods that those experts in yoga teach as the proper means. (10) The noble ones declare the slaughter of those who have laid down their weapons, those with disheveled hair, those with palms joined in supplication, and those who have turned their backs in retreat to be forbidden. (11)

The teacher should prescribe penance for those who have understood the scriptures but have fallen into error due to the weakness of their senses, according to their specific actions as previously described. (12) If they should persist excessively in transgressing the scriptures, he should bring them before the king. (13) The king [should bring them] before a domestic priest who is skilled in dharma and artha. (14) He [the priest] should appoint Brahmins [to oversee them]. (15) According to the degree of their offense, he should exhaust them through restrictive disciplines, with the exception of corporal punishment or slavery. (16)
Thus ends the tenth section in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

The king shall inflict punishment upon the other castes after having investigated their deeds until the loss of life. (1) He shall not inflict punishment when there is doubt. (2) Having thoroughly investigated the matter by means of divine ordeals, the king may proceed to inflict punishment. (3) A king who conducts himself in this manner conquers both worlds. (4)

The path belongs to the king when he has not met with a Brahmin; but when he has met with one, the path belongs to the Brahmin alone. [One must yield] to a vehicle, to one burdened by a load, to a sick person, and to a woman; thus it should be yielded by all. And [one must yield] to those who are superior by caste by means of the other castes. To those who are ill-mannered, fallen, intoxicated, or insane, the way must be yielded by everyone for the sake of their own safety.

Through righteous conduct, a lower caste attains each successive higher caste upon the transition of birth. Through unrighteous conduct, a higher caste falls to each successive lower caste upon the transition of birth.

One should not take another wife while his current wife is endowed with both virtue and offspring. (12) In the absence of either one, another may be taken before the establishment of the sacred fires. (13) For once the establishment of the fires has been performed, she becomes connected with the ritual acts of which this [wife] is a constituent part. (14)
One should not give one's daughter to a man of the same *gotra*. Nor [should one give her] to those who are related to the mother through the bond of birth.

In the Brāhma marriage, having ascertained the kinship, character, learning, and health [of the groom], one should bestow the daughter, after adorning her according to one's ability, for the sake of procreation and joint performance of duties. (17) In the Ārṣa marriage, a pair of cattle should be given to the father of the daughter. (18) In the Daiva marriage, one should bestow her upon the officiating priest during the course of a sacrifice. (19) When a couple unites through mutual desire, that is the Gāndharva marriage. (20)
Thus ends the eleventh section in the second book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.

If one should carry off [the bride] after giving wealth within the scope of one's power, that is the Āsura [form]. (1) If one should carry her off after deceiving the father who has a daughter, that is the Rākṣasa [form]. (2)
Of these, the first three are commended; each preceding one is superior to the next. (3) As the marriage is conducted, so the offspring becomes. (4)

One should not step upon anything gathered by hand that has not been sprinkled with water, even if it belongs to a Brāhmaṇa. (5) One should not pass between the sacred fire and a Brāhmaṇa. (6) Nor should one pass between [the fire] and several Brāhmaṇas. (7) Or, having asked for permission, one may pass through. (8)

One should not maintain fire and water simultaneously. (9) One should avoid the mixing together of various fires. (10) When fire is being brought toward oneself, one should not circumambulate it while it has not yet been established upon the ground. (11) And one should not join one's hands behind one's back. (12)

Having fallen asleep while the sun was setting, he shall remain seated for the night without eating and with his speech restrained. When morning has dawned, having touched water, he shall release his speech. (13) Having fallen asleep while the sun was rising, he shall remain standing for the day without eating and with his speech restrained. (14) According to some, he should restrain his breath until he is exhausted. (15) Or [he should do so] after seeing an evil dream. (16) Or when desiring to accomplish a purpose. (17) And also upon the transgression of any other rule. (18)

When there is doubt regarding the consequences of a fault, that [act] should not be performed. (19) Likewise with regard to what constitutes a day for study and what does not. (20) When in doubt, one should not speak as if one had direct perception. (21)

In the cases of one who causes the sun to set or rise while he is eating, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, an elder brother whose younger brother marries first, a younger brother who marries before his elder, one who has caused his elder brother to marry, one who has been superseded by a younger brother, one who has superseded his younger brother, and one who has been superseded by a younger brother—among these, for each subsequent person, the penance for the act of impurity is increasingly more severe. Regarding this, some say that after performing the specific mark of penance, the individual must be readmitted.
Thus ends the twelfth section in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

For those who approach their wife of equal caste, as prescribed by the ancient scriptures and according to the proper season, there is a connection with their sons through their ritual acts (karma). And there is no deviation from the inheritance for both [husband and wife]. 1–2.

There is fault in sexual intercourse with a woman who has not been previously married, with one who is unmarried, or with one of a different caste; even in those cases, the son born is indeed faulty. (3–4)
"For he is the son of the one who procreates," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, they cite this:
"O Janaka, it is only now that I am jealous of women, not before;
for when [the gods] declared in the abode of Yama that he was the son of the progenitor."
The depositor of semen leads his son away after death to the abode of Yama;
therefore, fearing the semen of others, men protect their wives.
"Be vigilant; guard this thread [of your lineage]. Let not others sow their seeds in your field.
In the life hereafter, the son belongs to the progenitor; the sower makes this thread of his own in vain. (6)

Transgression of the Dharma and rashness were observed among the ancients. Due to their extraordinary spiritual power, no sin accrued to them. One who emulates them without having examined that [power] perishes.

There is no such thing as the sale or the legal purchase of offspring. (10) Regarding marriage, it is heard in the sacred texts that for one who has a daughter, a gift may be given out of desire; however, for the sake of dharma, it is prescribed that one should give a hundred cows and a chariot to the father of the daughter. To say that one might do this "falsely" implies that the term "purchase" used in that context is merely a figurative expression of praise, for the relationship [between the two families] arises from dharma. (11)
Having satisfied the eldest with a single share of wealth. ||12||
Thus ends the thirteenth section in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

While living, one shall divide the inheritance equally among the sons, excluding the eunuch, the insane, and the outcast. (1) In the absence of sons, it goes to the nearest *sapiṇḍa*. (2) In his absence, the teacher; in the absence of the teacher, the pupil; having taken [the property], he shall employ it for those purposes or for religious duties. (3) Or the daughter. (4) In the absence of all these, the king shall take the inheritance. (5)

"According to some, the eldest son is the sole heir. [6] "In certain regions, gold, black cows, and black land belong to the eldest. [7] "A chariot and the household utensils of the father [belong to him]. [8] "Ornaments and the wealth of the wife's kinsmen [belong to him], according to some. [9] "That is contradicted by the sacred scriptures. [10] "It is heard in the Veda without qualification that Manu divided his inheritance among his sons. [11] "Nevertheless, it is also heard in one place: 'Therefore, they cause the eldest son to depart with the wealth. [12] "Furthermore, those who know the principles of logic say that this is a perpetual restatement (*nityānuvāda*) and not an injunction (*vidhi*), just as it is said: 'Therefore, goats and sheep move together among cattle'; 'Therefore, the mouth of a *snātaka* seems to hum'; and 'Therefore, the goat and the learned Brahmin are most desirous of women. [13] "For all who are endowed with righteousness (*dharma*) are entitled to a share. [14] "But even if he is the eldest, one should exclude from his share anyone who acquires property through unrighteousness. [15]

No division of property exists between husband and wife. (16) For from the taking of the hand, there is joint status in ritual acts. (17) Likewise in the fruits of meritorious deeds. (18) And in the possession of property. (19) Indeed, they do not teach that theft occurs when the husband is away on a journey or when making a gift for a specific occasion. (20)
Thus ends the fourteenth section in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
By this, the religious customs of regions and families are explained. ||1||

Upon the death of those related on the mother’s side and on the father’s side up to the seventh person, or as far as the relationship is known, there shall be the touching of water for purification; however, this excludes fetuses that have not yet reached one year of age. (2) Among these, the same applies to the mother and the father. (3) And the same applies to those who take [the property]. (4)

When a wife who was like a supreme guru has died, there shall be fasting until the time is past (the next morning). (5) They should assume the appearance of those afflicted by disease. (6) Having disheveled their hair, scattered dust [over themselves], and wearing a single garment, they face south, immerse themselves once, and having emerged, sit down. (7) In this manner, three times. (8) Having poured out water as a sign of that [death], they return to the village without looking back and do what women tell them to do. (9) Regarding other [deaths], some teachers teach exactly this same procedure. (10)
One should feed those who are pure and learned in the mantras at all ritual acts. (11) One bestows gifts by way of place, time, purity, and a worthy recipient. (12)

That which is not offered into the fire and the first portion of which is not given away should not be eaten. (13) There is no offering of alkaline substances or salt. (14) Likewise, there is none of inferior things or of mixed substances. (15) For that which is not fit for sacrifice, one should remove the hot ashes toward the north and offer therein; thus it becomes both offered and unoffered in the fire. (16)
A woman shall not offer the oblation. (17) Nor one who has not been initiated. (18)

Fetuses do not become impure from the time of the first feeding with solid food (annaprāśana). Some say until the completion of one year. Others say until they can no longer distinguish the directions. Another view holds that it is until the initiation ceremony (upanayana); for it is at this point that qualification according to the scriptures occurs. This is the established conclusion; and so too is the traditional law (smṛti).
Thus ends the fifteenth section in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the second book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.

In former times, gods and humans existed together in this world. Then, by means of their actions, the gods went to heaven and the humans were left behind. Those among them who undertake such actions come to exist in that other world together with the gods and Brahman. Now, Manu has proclaimed this rite under the name *śrāddha*, for the sake of the ultimate welfare of progeny. In this rite, the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) are the deities, while the Brahmins serve the purpose of the *āhavanīya* fire.
The rite should be performed month by month. (4) The afternoon of the dark fortnight is superior. (5) Likewise, the later days of the dark fortnight are preferable. (6)

By performing [the śrāddha] on any day of the dark fortnight (aparapakṣa), one gratifies the ancestors. However, for the performer, there is a distinction in the fruit resulting from the restriction of time. If performed on the first day, offspring consisting mostly of females are born. On the second, thieves; on the third, those endowed with Vedic splendor (brahmavarcas); on the fourth, one possessing small livestock; on the fifth, males—[one has] many children and does not die childless. On the sixth, one is habituated to travel and gambling; on the seventh, success in agriculture; on the eighth, prosperity; on the ninth, single-hoofed animals; on the tenth, success in trade; on the eleventh, iron, tin, and lead; on the twelfth, one possesses cattle. On the thirteenth, one has many sons, many friends, and handsome offspring, but they die young. On the fourteenth, success in weaponry; on the fifteenth, prosperity.

In this regard, the substances are sesame, beans, rice, barley, water, roots, and fruits. (23) However, when the food is oily, the gratification of the ancestors is more intense and lasts for a longer period. (24) Likewise, it is so when the substance has been acquired through righteous means and offered at a sacred site (*tīrtha*). (25) With beef, the gratification lasts for one year. (26) Even greater than that is the gratification from buffalo meat. (27) By this, the purity of the meat of domestic and wild animals is explained. (28)
Thus ends the sixteenth section in the second book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.
On a bed of swords, by means of the flesh of a rhinoceros, one attains infinite time; likewise by the flesh of the *śatabali* fish, and by that of the *vārdhrāṇasa*.

Being self-restrained and with a serene mind, he should feed invited Brahmins who are knowers of the Veda, provided they are not related by birth, lineage, mantra, or being a pupil. (4) However, if others possess deficient qualities, even a uterine brother who is superior should be fed. (5) By this, pupils are also explained [as being eligible]. (6)
Moreover, they also cite this: ||7||
The alms-food called *saṃbhojanī* is the food of the *piśācas*;
it goes neither to the ancestors nor to the gods.
Having its merit exhausted, it wanders right here in this world.
Like a cow that has lost her calf within the stall. ||8||

"Even while enjoying herself right here, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) causes one family to perish after another. (9) "Among those of equal qualities, one who is advanced in age is superior; even if poor in material wealth, he is desirable if he seeks [to give]. (10)

On the preceding day is the announcement; on the following day is the second [announcement]; the third is the formal invitation. Some teachers prescribe that the Śrāddha rite should be performed three times. As the first [is performed], so are the second and the third.

Having collected portions from all the food items in every respect, he should eat a mouthful at least of what remains, as previously prescribed. But according to the northern custom, water-vessels are brought to the hands of those who are already seated.

"Let the fire be drawn out, and let the offering be made," he addresses [the sacrificer]. "If you so desire, let it be drawn out; if you so desire, let the offering be made in the fire"—thus permitted, he may draw out the fire and offer the oblation.

They declare that the sight of dogs and those excluded from the community (*apapātra*) at a *śrāddha* is forbidden. (20) A leper, one afflicted with skin disease, one who approaches the bed of another’s wife, the son of a soldier, and one born to a Brāhmaṇa woman from a Śūdra—these, while eating at a *śrāddha*, become defilers of the row. (21) One who knows the *trimadhu*, the *trisuparṇa*, and the *triṇāciketa*; one who has performed the four *medha* sacrifices; one who maintains the five sacred fires; a singer of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*; one who has studied the Veda; the son of a learned teacher; and a *Śrotriya*—these, while eating at a *śrāddha*, become purifiers of the row. (22)
And one should not perform a *śrāddha* at night (23). And once it has begun, there shall be no eating until its completion (24), except during an eclipse of Rāhu (25).
Thus ends the seventeenth section in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the second book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.

One should avoid melted butter, churned curd, oil-cake, honey, and meat; (1) black grain, the food of a Śūdra, and whatever else is considered unfit to be eaten; (2) that which is not fit for an oblation, falsehood, anger, and anything by which one might provoke anger—one who desires memory, fame, intelligence, heaven, and nourishment should avoid these twelve things. (3)

Covering the area from below the navel to above the knees, touching water at the three periods of the day, subsisting on food not cooked over fire, avoiding the shade, and remaining either standing or sitting, one should observe this vow for a year. This is said to be equivalent to forty-eight years.

The daily *śrāddha* (5). Outside the village, those who are pure prepare [the food] in a pure place (6). Therein are new materials (7)—those by which the food is prepared and those upon which it is eaten (8). And he should give these to those who have eaten (9). He should also feed those who are eminent (10). And he should not give the leavings to one who does not possess those qualities (11). Thus for a year (12). For them, the best [form] should be performed with iron and a goat (13). And he should have a measuring-vessel made that is concealed (14). In its northern half, he should feed the Brahmins (15). They teach that he sees both: the Brahmins eating and the ancestors in the measuring-vessel (16). From this point forward, it is optional whether the rite is performed or not (17). For through the *śrāddha*, the ancestors experience satisfaction (18).
One desiring prosperity [should sacrifice] under Tiṣya. ||19||
Thus ends the eighteenth section in the second book of the *Āpastambīya Dharmasūtra*.

Having had white mustard seeds ground into powder, he should wash his hands and feet with them, rinse his mouth, and touch his ears. Then, sitting on a seat where the wind does not blow strongly, he should eat while maintaining silence, facing south, using the skin of a goat as his first option. They teach that eating while facing in this manner is detrimental to one's lifespan for his mother. A ladle made of udumbara wood with a golden center is recommended. No one else should eat from it. He should take up as much food as fits in a single mouthful; he should not let it spill; he should not drop it; or, if he drops it, [he should not do so again].

One should swallow the entire morsel together with the thumb. (9) One should not make a sound with the mouth. (10) Nor should one shake the hand. (11) Having sipped water, one should hold the hands raised until they become wet. (12) Then one should touch fire. (13) During the day, one should not eat anything other than roots and fruits. (14) One should avoid food intended for the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice and similar offerings. (15) One should eat while wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and covered by an upper garment. (16)

But at the *naiyamika* śrāddha, one should offer food accompanied by fat. (17) Ghee and meat constitute the primary rule. (18) In their absence, oil and vegetables [are the substitutes]. (19) During the *maghā* asterisms, one should feed the Brahmins with ghee according to the ritual procedure for the śrāddha. (20)
Thus ends the nineteenth section in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

At the monthly *śrāddha*, one should employ a *droṇa* of sesame seeds by whatever means possible that one is able to do. One should feed those who possess the requisite qualities, and they should not give their leftovers to someone who lacks such qualities.

During the northern course of the sun, having fasted for at least one night during the waxing fortnight, one who desires prosperity should cook a *sthālīpāka* under the asterism Tiṣya, sacrifice to Mahārāja, feed a Brāhmaṇa with that [food] mixed with clarified butter, and have him recite for the sake of prosperity the words of success. 3.

In this manner, day after day, until the next Tiṣya constellation; two [mouthfuls] on the second day; three on the third; thus for a year by gradual increase. He nourishes a great abundance. Fasting begins from the very first day.

One should avoid eating in the presence of those who possess superior splendor (10). One should avoid standing upon ashes or chaff (11). One should avoid washing one foot with the other and standing upon it (12). One should avoid swinging the feet about (13). One should avoid resting the shank upon the knee (14). One should avoid scratching the nails with the fingernails (15). One should avoid cracking the finger-joints without cause (16). And whatever else is censured by the wise, that too one should avoid (17).

He is a provider for those engaged in dharma and for the acquisition of property; he is a bestower at a sacred ford; he is a driver away from what is not a sacred ford, so that there may be no fear; he is a gatherer of men; and he is an enjoyer of pleasures that are not forbidden by dharma. Thus, he conquers both worlds.
Thus ends the twentieth section in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

There are four stages of life: that of the householder, that of the teacher’s family, that of the silent sage, and that of the forest-dweller. (1) By conducting oneself with undistracted attention in all of these according to the instruction, one attains security. (2) For all of them, residence in the teacher’s family begins from the initiation ceremony. (3) For all of them, there is no relinquishment of sacred knowledge. (4) Having understood the ritual acts, one may undertake whichever one desires. (5)
Just as there is a rule for one whose purpose is knowledge, by this very means he reaches the end: the casting off of the body in the teacher’s household by the religious student (brahmacārin). 6.

Now, concerning the wandering mendicants (parivrāja): ||7|| For this very reason, one who is still a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) goes forth [into the life of renunciation]. ||8|| To him they teach [the following]: ||9||
The sage should be without fire, without a dwelling, without shelter, and without refuge.

Only engaged in the private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*), having abandoned speech and obtained his livelihood for the vital breaths (*prāṇavṛtti*) in the village, he should live without sacrificial fires and without a home in this world or the next. (10) A garment that has been discarded is prescribed for him. (11) Some [prescribe] complete liberation from all things. (12) Having abandoned truth and falsehood, pleasure and pain, the Vedas, this world, and the next, one should seek the Self (*ātman*). (13) When it is realized, there is the attainment of security (*kṣema*). (14)

That is contradicted by the scriptures. (15) If the attainment of security occurred upon awakening, one would not experience suffering even here in this very life. (16) By this, the subsequent [point] is explained. (17)
Now, the forest-dweller (vānaprastha). ||18|| For this very reason, one who has observed the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya) goes forth (pravrajati). ||19|| To him they teach [the following]. ||20||
The sage should maintain a single fire, have no fixed abode, and be without shelter or refuge.
He should continue his private recitation even while releasing his speech. ||21||
Thus ends the twenty-first section in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
A garment made of forest bark was prescribed for him. ||1||

Then one should live subsisting on roots, fruits, leaves, and grasses. (2) Finally, one should subsist on [these] as they become available. (3) Then one should resort to water, air, and space. (4) Among these, each subsequent practice is superior in its result. (5)

Alternatively, some teach the following sequence specifically for the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*): [6] Having completed his studies, taken a wife, and established the sacred fires, he undertakes those ritual acts which are prescribed as being no later than the *Soma* sacrifice. [7] Having built a house, he should dwell outside the village together with his wife, his offspring, and his fires; [8] or he may live alone. [9] He should subsist by gathering grains from the ground or by gleaning ears of corn. [10] From this point forward, he must not accept gifts. [11] And when he has performed the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), he should offer oblations. [12] He should descend into the water slowly, striking it gently, and touch the water while facing the sun. [13] This is the rule for touching water in all cases. [14]

They prescribe a single pair of items for him from among those used for cooking and eating: an axe, a hatchet, and a sickle. (15) Taking one from each of these pairs and giving away the others, he should dwell in the forest. (16) From that point forward, his fire-oblation, livelihood, waiting for alms, and clothing shall be provided solely by the forest. (17) In those rites where there are *puroḍāśa* cakes, they should be made of wild grains (*caru*). (18) Everything, including the private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*), should be performed in a low voice. (19) He should not call out for attention in the forest. (20) A shelter for the sake of the sacred fires [is permitted]. (21) He himself should live in the open air. (22) His bed and seat should be on the bare ground. (23) When new grain has arrived, he may permit the use of old grain. (24)
Thus ends the twenty-second section in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

Or, desiring a more extensive discipline, he should fetch his sustenance day by day with a bowl, both morning and evening. Then, subsisting on roots, fruits, leaves, and grasses, he should practice; finally, he should resort to whatever is naturally available, and thereafter to water, air, and space. Among these, each subsequent practice is superior to the preceding one in its result.
Now, they cite two verses from the Purāṇas: ||3||
The eighty-eight thousand seers who desired offspring took the southern path of Aryaman and entered the cremation grounds. (4)
The eighty-eight thousand seers who led their progeny along the northern path of Aryaman indeed attain immortality. ||5||

Thus ends the praise of those who have sublimated their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas). Furthermore, there are also those for whom success is achieved through mere intention (saṃkalpa). For example: [the ability to bring] rain, the granting of offspring, vision from afar, swiftness like thought, and whatever else is of a similar nature. Therefore, because they are based on sacred revelation and because their fruits are perceptible, some declare these stages of life (āśrama) to be superior.

For those who are advanced in the three Vedas, the Vedas alone are the final authority. In that regard, they consider any practice to be without authority if it contradicts what is heard in the Vedas concerning rice, barley, animals, clarified butter, milk, sacrificial vessels, and the wife—specifically the injunctions that rites should be performed loudly or softly. As for what is called the "cremation ground," this is prescribed as the final purification of the person at the conclusion of various rituals. Beyond that, an eternal fruit is heard of in the Vedas, designated by the term "heaven."
Thus ends the twenty-third section in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

Moreover, the sacred tradition declares his immortality through progeny: "Through offspring you are born again; that, O mortal, is your immortality. (1) Furthermore, this very same person is perceived separately when grown, and a similarity is observed; only the physical body is different. (2) Those who abide in their prescribed duties increase the fame and the heavenly realm of their ancestors after death. (3) In this way, each subsequent generation benefits those preceding them. (4) Until the dissolution of all beings, they remain victors in heaven. (5) At the time of re-creation, they become the seeds [of the new creation], according to the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*. (6) Moreover, there is the word of Prajāpati: (7)
The threefold knowledge, the life of sacred study, procreation, faith, austerity, sacrifice, and the giving of gifts—
those who perform these, with them indeed we are.
Becoming like dust, he perishes while praising another. ||8||

In that regard, those who have committed evil perish like a leaf from a tree; they do not harm others. (9) For him, there is no connection with actions in this world, nor with the fruits of actions in the next world. (10) This is to be understood by means of this. (11) This is the creation of Prajāpati and the seers. (12) In that regard, for those who have performed meritorious deeds, their subtle bodies (*prakṛti*) are perceived as blazing intensely. (13)

It may be that someone, through a portion of their karma or through austerity, conquers a finite world while still embodied and attains the fulfillment of their will; yet that is not the preeminence of the stages of life.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the second book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.
The general and specific duties of all social classes have been explained. Now, however, we shall describe those of the king specifically. ||1||

One should cause the house and the city to be measured out with the gate facing south. (2) The house is within the city. (3) In front of that is the guest-house; they call that the place of reception. (4) To the south of the city is the assembly hall, with its entrance toward the south or the north, so that both the exterior and the interior are visible. (5)
In all these cases, the sacred fires should be maintained perpetually; and the worship of the fire should be constant, just as it is for a householder.

In the guest-house, he should lodge guests who are at least as learned as those well-versed in the Vedas (śrotriya). For them, lodgings, beds, food, and drink should be provided according to their merit.

One should not live beyond the means of one's teachers or ministers. Furthermore, within his domain, no one should perish from hunger, disease, cold, or heat, whether due to a lack of resources or through intentional neglect.

In the middle of the assembly hall, having raised up the gaming-ground and sprinkled it with water, one should cast down an even number of Vibhītaka dice according to the requirements. Noble men, pure and of truthful character, shall be the players.
The taking up of weapons, dancing, singing, and instrumental music shall not exist except for those dependent upon the king. 14.
The king is a creator of security in whose realm—whether in the village or the forest—no fear of thieves exists. ||15||
Thus ends the twenty-fifth section in the second book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.

By bestowing fields and wealth upon Brahmins according to their merit, without causing hardship to his dependents, he conquers infinite worlds. (1) They say that a king who is slain while seeking to recover the property of Brahmins is a sacrifice in which his own body is the sacrificial post and his life is the infinite sacrificial fee. (2) By this, other heroes are also explained: those who cast off their bodies while fighting for a righteous cause. (3)

In villages and cities, he should appoint noble, pure, and truthful men for the protection of the subjects. Their attendants should likewise possess those same qualities. A city extending for one *yojana* in every direction must be protected from thieves; a village for one *krośa*. Whatever is stolen therein by them [the thieves] shall be made good by those [attendants].

He shall collect the lawful tax. (9) A *śrotriya* is exempt from taxes. (10) So too are the women of all castes. (11) And boys before the appearance of secondary sexual characteristics. (12) And those who dwell for the sake of learning. (13) And ascetics who are devoted to dharma. (14) And a *śūdra* who is a foot-washer. (15) And those afflicted by blindness, muteness, deafness, or disease. (16) And those who have become useless through the possession of property. (17)

If a young man, though adorned, enters another's wife's quarters or approaches an unmarried girl unintentionally, he should be restrained by a verbal reprimand. But if he does so intentionally with a wicked disposition, he shall be punished.

When a sexual union has occurred, there shall be the excision of the penis together with the testicles. (20) But in the case of a maiden, having seized her own [belongings], she should be banished. (21) Now, in the case of a servant, [the punishment] shall be by the king. (22) And from this point forward, [the woman] must be protected from sexual intercourse. (23) However, when a means of atonement has been accepted, he should deliver her back to her masters. (24)
Thus ends the twenty-sixth section in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
For through conduct according to the Dharma as before, there is indeed a connection. ||1||

One should not disclose to others a woman who belongs to the same lineage (*sagotra*). For they teach that a woman is given away for the sake of the family. That [practice] has been subverted due to the weakness of the senses. For the status of being "another's" (*paratva*) is no different regarding the hand [in marriage]. Indeed, upon the violation of that [rule], both [parties] go to hell. For the greater spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*) results from such an undertaking through the offspring born of a formal commitment (*niyama*).

An Ārya who has intercourse with a Śūdra woman shall be banished; a Śūdra who has intercourse with an Ārya woman shall be put to death. Furthermore, he shall cause her to be emaciated by hard labor. They teach that when there is a single instance of sexual union with a woman of the same caste who has previously belonged to another, one quarter of the penance for loss of caste (pātitya) falls upon him. Likewise, for each repetition, a quarter falls; at the fourth repetition, the whole [penalty] applies.

The tongue shall be cut off for a Śūdra who insults an Ārya who is righteous. (14) For [insulting] him while speaking, walking on the same path, lying on the same bed, or sitting on the same seat, he shall receive a flogging with a rod until he becomes equal [in status]. (15) In cases of killing a man, theft, or seizing land, he shall be put to death after his own property has been confiscated. (16)

But for a Brahmin among these, there shall be the destruction of his sight. (17) He shall impose the transgression of the rules or bind him in secret. (18) This continues until [the offense] is completed. (19) If it is not completed, he is to be expelled. (20) An Ācārya, an officiating priest, a Snātaka, or a king may provide protection, except in the case of one deserving death. (21)
Thus ends the twenty-seventh section in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the second book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.

If, after taking possession of a field, there is no harvest due to a lack of effort, he who was prosperous shall be liable for that loss. (1) For an indolent farmer who abandons his work, there is punishment by flogging. (2) The same applies to a herdsman. (3) And there shall be confinement of his cattle. (4) One who leaves the pen at dawn shall be made to emaciate the cattle; he shall not let them perish. (5) If, having confined the cattle, they die or are lost, he shall restore them to their owners. (6)

If, through negligence, he sees cattle released in the forest, he shall bring them to the village and return them to their owners. (7) If negligence occurs again, he shall confine them once more. (8) Beyond that, he shall not neglect them. (9)

An ignorant man who takes another’s property—whether firewood, water, roots, flowers, fruits, perfumes, food, or vegetables—is to be restrained by verbal censure. (10) But for a learned man, there shall be the seizure of his garment. (11) Furthermore, he is not to be punished if he takes food out of necessity when his life is in danger. (12)
When the occasion for punishment has arisen, the sin touches the king if he fails to act. ||13||
Thus ends the twenty-eighth section in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

The instigator, the advisor, and the doer share in the results of actions that lead to heaven or hell. (1) Among these, he who contributes most to the undertaking receives a greater portion of the result. (2)
The two householders are the masters of the wealth. With their permission, others also may act for the benefit of that [wealth]. ||3-4||

In a dispute, those who are endowed with learning and noble birth, who are aged, wise, and unerring in matters of dharma [should decide]; in a case of doubt, having deliberated by means of signs and divine methods. ||5-6||

On an auspicious day, in the morning, when the fire has been kindled, at the edge of the water, having had both parties heard by a royal official, the chief witness shall, with the consent of all, state the truth in response to the question. (7) If he speaks untruth, the king shall inflict punishment. (8) Furthermore, in the life hereafter, there is additionally hell for him. (9) For truth, there is heaven and the praise of all beings. (10)
That which is found among women and Śūdras is the ultimate limit of knowledge; they teach that this is the supplement of the Atharvaveda.

The completion of dharma is difficult to achieve through what is traditionally handed down; rather, it is accomplished through the practice of its defining characteristics. In this regard, the defining characteristic is as follows: one should conform to the conduct of the noble ones—those who are consistently composed, well-disciplined, aged, self-possessed, free from greed, and devoid of hypocrisy—in all inhabited lands. In this way, one conquers both worlds.
"One should learn the remaining rules of dharma from women and from members of all social classes," so say some; thus [it is] according to some. 15.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth section in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the second book of the *Āpastambīya-dharmasūtra*.
Thus ends the second question.
And thus the Dharmasūtra of Āpastamba is completed.
